# ExoStride Singapore — full text

Source: https://exostride.sg · Last updated 2026-08-19 · Languages: en-SG, zh-Hans-SG

## Product summary

ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a 2.4 kg powered hip exoskeleton sold in Singapore by HT Science & Development Pte. Ltd. It senses your gait and delivers up to 16 Nm of adaptive assistance at the hip, removing up to 80% of the lower-body load per step, cutting climbing energy by up to 35% and daily commute exertion by 30–50%. It runs up to 4 hours per 2-hour charge, is IP54-rated for rain and dust, folds, and starts on one button with no app. It is worn over clothing and used at home, on trails or on the commute without a prescription.

### Specifications

- Peak assist torque: 16 Nm
- Weight: 2.4 kg
- Ingress protection: IP54
- Assistance per charge: Up to 4 h
- Full charge: 2 h
- Power on: One button, no app
- Modes: Terrain-adaptive
- Portability: Foldable

## Frequently asked questions

### What is ExoStride and who makes it?

ExoStride is a powered hip exoskeleton made by HT Science. The model sold in Singapore is the US-H-1.0Pro, distributed exclusively by HT Science & Development Pte. Ltd. (UEN 202033252G001).

Pricing is quoted directly by the Singapore team, since it depends on configuration and fitting. Message +65 9122 7009 on WhatsApp or call +65 8355 0979 for a current figure.

### Is ExoStride a medical device?

No. It is a consumer mobility-assist exoskeleton used for rehabilitation support, outdoor activity and everyday walking. It is worn at home without a prescription and does not diagnose or treat any condition.

### How heavy is it and does it need an app?

2.4 kg, foldable, and one-button — no app or setup is needed to simply walk.

### How long does the battery last?

Up to 4 hours of assistance on a 2-hour full charge. Stairs and steep gradients draw more than flat ground.

### Can I use it in the rain?

Yes. It is IP54-rated — dust-protected and resistant to splashing water from any direction, which covers typical Singapore rain. Avoid full submersion.

### Where can I try ExoStride in Singapore?

Fittings are done on your own route — at home, on a trail such as Bukit Timah or MacRitchie, or on your actual commute. Book via the form on this page or WhatsApp +65 9122 7009.

### Who is ExoStride for?

Three groups: people in rehabilitation or with reduced mobility, hikers and outdoor enthusiasts, and urban commuters who walk stair-heavy routes daily.

## Guides

### Aging in place with a powered exoskeleton: what changes at home

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/aging-in-place-powered-exoskeleton/

Question: Can a powered exoskeleton help an older adult stay living at home?

Answer: Yes. A powered hip exoskeleton like the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro removes up to 80% of the lower-body load from each step and adds up to 16 Nm of assistance exactly when the hip lifts. That is usually the difference between managing the stairs, the walk to the market and the afternoon stroll — and giving them up. It weighs 2.4 kg, folds, needs no app, and is worn over normal clothing at home without a prescription.

#### What aging in place actually breaks down to

Staying at home is rarely lost in one dramatic moment. It is lost one route at a time. The stairs to the flat become a negotiation. The walk to the wet market gets shortened, then dropped. The afternoon stroll becomes a chair by the window. Each is small; together they are the whole question of whether someone still lives their own life in their own home.

- Stairs and kerbs — the first routes to go.
- Distance — the market, the coffee shop, the clinic.
- Confidence — the fear of the fall arrives before the fall.

#### How a powered hip exoskeleton changes those routes

The US-H-1.0Pro is not a fixed-speed motor strapped to a belt. It reads the gait and adds torque at the moment the hip flexes — the muscle group that actually costs the most on a stair or an incline. Practically, that means:

- Up to 80% less lower-body pressure, or 3–5x less load per step.
- One button. Assistance begins the moment they stand — no app, no menu, nothing to learn.
- Posture detection pauses assistance when they sit, and resumes when they rise.
- 2.4 kg and foldable — lighter than a bag of groceries, and it stows by the door.

#### Restoration, not replacement

This is the line that matters, and it is the one the category keeps getting wrong. A wheelchair replaces walking. A powered hip exoskeleton keeps the person walking — their own gait, their own legs, their own pace, with the hardest 80% of each step taken off the top. Mobility restoration for older and recovering users is the first thing ExoStride was built for, not an afterthought bolted onto an adventure product.

#### A realistic first fortnight

Nobody should go from the sofa to a five-kilometre walk. A guided fitting sets the assistance level, and the first two weeks usually look like this:

- Days 1–3 — flat ground indoors and the corridor, 10–15 minutes.
- Days 4–7 — one flight of stairs, then the lift lobby and back.
- Week 2 — the route that was given up first. Usually the market.

FAQ:

- Q: Is ExoStride a medical device?
  A: No. The US-H-1.0Pro is a consumer mobility-assist exoskeleton for rehabilitation, outdoor and everyday use. It supports mobility restoration and is used at home without a prescription. It does not diagnose or treat a condition, and it is not a substitute for physiotherapy — many users do both.
- Q: How heavy is it for an older person to put on?
  A: 2.4 kg in total, worn at the waist so the weight sits on the pelvis rather than the shoulders. Most users can put it on seated in under a minute after the fitting session.
- Q: Does it need a phone or an app to work?
  A: No. One button starts assistance. The app is optional and is only used for settings — walking never requires it.
- Q: Will it work on HDB stairs and kerbs?
  A: Yes — stairs are where the assistance is most noticeable. Terrain-adaptive mode switching raises assistance on steps and inclines and eases off on level ground, automatically.
- Q: Can it be used in the rain?
  A: Yes. IP54 covers dust ingress and splashing water from any direction, which includes typical Singapore rain. Avoid full submersion.

### Buying an exoskeleton for a parent: a caregiver's guide

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-for-elderly-parent-caregiver-guide/

Question: How do I choose a powered exoskeleton for an elderly parent?

Answer: Check five things, in this order: (1) where they actually struggle — stairs, distance or confidence; (2) total worn weight, because anything above roughly 3 kg gets left by the door; (3) whether assistance starts on one button with no app; (4) whether the assistance adapts to stairs automatically; and (5) whether you can book a supervised fitting in their own home rather than a showroom. ExoStride's US-H-1.0Pro is 2.4 kg, one-button, terrain-adaptive, and fitted at home in Singapore.

#### Start with the route, not the product

Before comparing any specification, name the specific journey that is being lost. "Mum is slower" is not actionable. "Mum has stopped going to the market on Saturday because of the overhead bridge" is. The route tells you which capability matters, and it is also the only honest way to judge, three weeks later, whether the thing worked.

#### The five checks

In practice these separate a device that gets worn from one that gets stored:

- Worn weight. Above ~3 kg, compliance drops sharply. US-H-1.0Pro is 2.4 kg, carried on the pelvis.
- Time to start. One button beats any app. If it needs a phone, it will not be used on a Tuesday morning.
- Stair behaviour. Ask to see it on an actual staircase, not a showroom ramp.
- Battery honesty. 4 hours of assistance and a 2-hour recharge should cover a full day of errands with margin.
- Where the fitting happens. A home fitting on their own stairs is worth more than any brochure.

#### How to raise it without it landing as an insult

This is the part most guides skip, and it is the part that decides the outcome. A mobility aid offered as a concession to decline gets refused. The same device offered as a way to get a specific thing back is usually accepted. Lead with the route — the market, the grandchild's school gate, the temple stairs — and let the hardware be the boring means to it. Ask them to try it once, on their own route, with no commitment.

FAQ:

- Q: What if my parent refuses to try it?
  A: Very common. It usually softens when the ask is a single trial on a route they miss, with no purchase attached. A supervised home fitting is designed for exactly that — the team brings it, fits it, walks the route with them, and leaves.
- Q: Is it safe for someone recovering from hip or knee surgery?
  A: Talk to their surgeon or physiotherapist first — post-operative loading is a clinical decision, not a product one. Many users introduce it after clearance to weight-bear, alongside physiotherapy rather than instead of it.
- Q: Can two people in the same household share one unit?
  A: Physically yes — the belt and thigh links adjust. In practice, sizing gets readjusted each swap, which adds friction. If both people would use it daily, raise it at the fitting.
- Q: What does a fitting in Singapore involve?
  A: A team member from HT Science & Development Pte. Ltd. — the exclusive Singapore seller — brings the unit to the home, sizes it, sets the assistance level and walks the chosen route with the user. Typically under an hour.

### Exoskeleton vs cane, walking frame and wheelchair: what each restores

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-vs-walking-frame-cane-wheelchair/

Question: What is the difference between an exoskeleton, a cane, a walking frame and a wheelchair?

Answer: They solve four different problems. A cane restores balance and costs you a hand. A walking frame restores stability but shortens stride and rules out stairs. A wheelchair restores distance by replacing walking altogether. A powered hip exoskeleton restores the effort itself — it leaves the natural gait intact, keeps both hands free, works on stairs, and removes up to 80% of the lower-body load per step. Choose by what is actually failing: balance, stability, distance or effort.

#### The comparison, honestly

None of these is a better version of the others. They intervene at different points:

- Cane — restores balance and a reference point. Costs one hand. Does nothing about effort.
- Walking frame — restores stability and confidence. Costs both hands, shortens stride, and stairs are out.
- Wheelchair — restores distance and removes fall risk, by replacing walking. Muscle and bone loading go with it.
- Powered hip exoskeleton — restores effort. Natural gait, both hands free, stairs included, up to 80% less load per step.

#### Which one, for which failure

A quick way to sort it: if the problem is wobble, the answer is a cane or frame. If the problem is that walking has become impossible or unsafe at any distance, the answer is a wheelchair. If the problem is that walking is still possible but has become too expensive — the stairs are managed but cost the rest of the afternoon — that is the specific gap a powered hip exoskeleton fills. It is not a stronger cane and it is not a lighter wheelchair.

#### They are not mutually exclusive

Plenty of users pair an exoskeleton with a cane: the exoskeleton handles the effort, the cane handles the balance reference. Others use a wheelchair for long outings and the exoskeleton for the home, the block and the stairs. Framing it as a ladder — cane, then frame, then chair — is what makes people resist the middle steps.

FAQ:

- Q: Does an exoskeleton reduce fall risk like a frame does?
  A: Differently. A frame reduces falls by adding external support points. An exoskeleton reduces the fatigue and hip weakness that cause many late-day stumbles, and keeps both hands free to grab a rail. It does not provide a static support point — if balance itself is the primary problem, a cane or frame still has a role.
- Q: Is it more expensive than a wheelchair?
  A: It sits in a different bracket from a basic cane or frame. Pricing for Singapore is quoted at the fitting by HT Science & Development Pte. Ltd. — message the team for a current figure.
- Q: Will using it make muscles weaker over time?
  A: It assists the hip flexors rather than replacing the movement, so the user is still walking under their own power with a portion of the load removed. Many users report walking more, not less. If deconditioning is a specific clinical concern, raise it with a physiotherapist.

### What 16 Nm of hip torque actually does for your body

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/hip-torque-16nm-explained/

Question: How much torque does a powered hip exoskeleton need?

Answer: Torque is rotational force at the joint. At the hip, 16 Nm is roughly the assistance of a firm, well-timed push at the thigh on every stride. It is not enough to move a leg that cannot move — and it is not meant to be. It is enough to remove the peak cost of a step, which is where a stair, a slope or the fourth kilometre actually hurts. Peak numbers matter far less than timing: assistance delivered at the wrong moment is dead weight.

#### What a newton-metre is, without the physics lecture

One newton-metre is the twist you get from pressing with about 1 kg of force at the end of a 10 cm lever. Sixteen of them, applied at the hip joint, is comparable to a steady hand pushing your thigh forward and up at the exact instant your leg starts to swing. You still do the walking. The assistance shaves the top off the hardest part.

#### Why the hip, and not the knee

On stairs and inclines, the hip flexors do the expensive work of lifting the whole leg against gravity; the knee mostly manages the landing. Assisting the hip therefore buys more per newton-metre and per gram of hardware, which is how the whole unit stays at 2.4 kg. It also leaves the knee's natural shock absorption untouched.

#### Timing beats peak numbers

This is the part the spec sheets never cover. A higher peak torque delivered 100 milliseconds late feels like a shove, fights your stride and gets switched off within a week. The US-H-1.0Pro reads gait continuously and releases torque inside the flexion window, and it shifts profile automatically between level ground, stairs and steep terrain. That is why there is nothing to adjust while walking.

#### What it adds up to

Measured across the three use cases ExoStride is built for:

- Rehabilitation — up to 80% less lower-body pressure per step.
- Climbs — up to 35% less energy on steep, sustained ascents.
- Daily commute — 30–50% less exertion across a normal day.

FAQ:

- Q: Is more torque always better?
  A: No. Beyond what the joint actually needs, extra torque adds motor mass, battery drain and a shoving sensation. For hip assistance in walking, stairs and hiking, correctly-timed torque in the 15–20 Nm range does the work; the differentiator is control, not the headline number.
- Q: Can I feel 16 Nm, or is it subtle?
  A: On level ground it is subtle — most users describe it as the ground being slightly downhill. On stairs and slopes it is unmistakable, because that is where the assistance profile ramps up.
- Q: Does higher assistance drain the battery faster?
  A: Yes, and terrain does too — a stair-heavy day draws more than flat ground. The 4-hour assist figure reflects mixed real-world use, with a 2-hour full recharge.

### Exoskeleton battery life: what 4 hours of assist really covers

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-battery-life-explained/

Question: How long does a powered exoskeleton battery last?

Answer: The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro delivers up to 4 hours of assistance and recharges fully in 2 hours. Because assistance is delivered on demand rather than continuously, that 4 hours is 4 hours of assisted walking — not 4 hours of being switched on. For most people that is a full commute plus errands, or a standard day hike, with margin. Stairs and steep gradients draw more than flat ground.

#### Hours are the wrong unit — terrain is the real one

Every brand quotes hours because hours are comparable on a spec sheet. In practice, an exoskeleton spends energy per assisted step, and steps are not equal. A flat MRT concourse costs a fraction of what a covered overhead bridge costs. Read any battery claim as a range shaped by the ground you actually walk on.

#### Three realistic days

Roughly what 4 hours of assistance covers:

- A Singapore commute — two station interchanges, an overhead bridge and both last-mile walks, twice a day, with margin left.
- A day of errands — market, clinic, coffee shop, and the walk back up to the flat.
- A day hike — a MacRitchie boardwalk loop or a Southern Ridges traverse; a sustained Bukit Timah climb will draw harder.

#### Charging habits that matter more than capacity

A 2-hour full recharge is short enough to change how you think about it. Charge it while you are at the desk, not overnight, and it is effectively always full. For long days, the honest advice is to plan the assistance rather than ration it — walk assisted on the stairs and the gradients, and let it idle on the flat, which the terrain-adaptive mode already does for you.

FAQ:

- Q: Can the battery be swapped mid-hike?
  A: Ask at the fitting — swap options depend on the configuration supplied in Singapore. For multi-day trips, plan a charge point rather than assuming a swap.
- Q: Does it still work with a flat battery?
  A: It stops assisting, but it does not lock your legs — you keep walking normally, carrying 2.4 kg. It never becomes an obstacle.
- Q: Does heat and humidity affect battery life?
  A: Sustained heat affects any lithium battery's output. In Singapore conditions the practical effect is modest; storing it in a hot car boot is worse for it than using it in the sun.

### IP54 explained: what tropical-grade sealing means for an exoskeleton

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/ip54-rating-tropical-climate/

Question: What does an IP54 rating mean, and is it rain-proof?

Answer: IP54 means two things. The 5 is dust: dust cannot enter in a quantity that interferes with operation. The 4 is water: protected against splashing water from any direction. In practice that covers a Singapore afternoon downpour, a humid platform, and trail dust — but not submersion, not a pressure hose, and not being left in a puddle. For a device you are meant to wear every day, IP54 is the difference between one that goes out in the rain and one that stays home.

#### Reading the two digits

IP stands for Ingress Protection, and the digits are independent:

- First digit (5) — solids. Dust-protected: some ingress is allowed, but not enough to affect operation.
- Second digit (4) — liquids. Protected against water splashed from any direction, tested from every angle.
- What it does not certify — immersion (that starts at 7), pressure jets (6), or long-term standing water.

#### Why this rating matters more here

In a temperate climate an unsealed device is inconvenient. In Singapore it is unusable. Rain arrives without much notice, most walking routes include an unsheltered stretch, and ambient humidity sits high enough year-round that condensation is a real consideration for any powered wearable. Sealing is not a premium feature here; it is the entry requirement.

#### Living with it sensibly

Walk in the rain; do not wade. Wipe it down and let it air-dry rather than sealing it damp into a bag. Trail dust and sweat salt are handled by the same rating, but a rinse after a coastal or beach walk is still sensible. None of this adds weight — the unit is still 2.4 kg with the sealing in place.

FAQ:

- Q: Can I wear it in a Singapore downpour?
  A: Yes. IP54 covers splashing water from any direction, which includes heavy rain while walking. Avoid full submersion and do not wade through standing water above the unit.
- Q: Can I rinse it under a tap?
  A: A light rinse and a wipe is fine. A pressure jet is not — that requires IPx6, which IP54 does not claim.
- Q: Did the sealing make it heavier or bulkier?
  A: No. It remains 2.4 kg and foldable.

### Powered hip assist for stairs: MRT stations, bridges and HDB blocks

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/powered-hip-assist-for-stairs/

Question: Can a powered exoskeleton help with climbing stairs?

Answer: Yes — stairs are the single clearest case for hip assistance. Climbing a step means lifting your whole body mass against gravity using the hip flexors, which is why stairs cost several times what flat ground costs. The US-H-1.0Pro detects the change in terrain and raises its assistance profile automatically, delivering up to 16 Nm at the moment of lift. Both hands stay free for the handrail.

#### Why stairs cost so much more than they look

On flat ground, walking is mostly a controlled fall forward — gravity does a share of the work. On a staircase, none of it is free. Every step raises your entire body mass by 15–18 cm, and the hip flexors carry that lift. This is why a two-flight climb can end a walk that a kilometre of flat pavement would not have.

#### The three staircases that matter in Singapore

The routes people actually give up first:

- Station stairs — Dhoby Ghaut, Bras Basah, Bencoolen and every deep interchange where the escalator queue is longer than the climb.
- Overhead bridges — unavoidable, unsheltered, and the reason many shorter routes get abandoned entirely.
- The walk up to the flat — the last flight, at the end of the day, carrying something.

#### What the exoskeleton actually does on a step

Sensors read the gait change as the leg begins a higher swing and the controller shifts to the stair profile — more torque, delivered earlier in the flexion window. Coming down, assistance eases so it does not push you into the descent. There is no stair button and nothing to switch. Both hands stay free, which matters more than any specification: the handrail is still the best safety device on a staircase.

FAQ:

- Q: Does it help going down as well as up?
  A: It assists the ascent, where the energy cost is. On descent it reduces assistance so it never pushes you forward — descent is a control problem, not a power problem, and the handrail remains the primary aid.
- Q: Is it safe on wet station stairs?
  A: The unit is IP54-rated so rain is not an issue for the device. Traction is still down to your footwear and the handrail — an exoskeleton assists effort, not grip.
- Q: Can I try it on real stairs before buying?
  A: Yes, and you should. Fittings in Singapore are done on the user's own route — their block, their station, their overhead bridge.

### What 30–50% less exertion feels like on a Singapore commute

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-daily-commute-singapore/

Question: Is a powered exoskeleton practical for a daily commute?

Answer: For a walking-heavy commute, yes. The US-H-1.0Pro reduces exertion by 30–50% across a normal day, weighs 2.4 kg, folds under a desk, needs no app and is IP54-rated for rain. It is worn over clothing at the waist and reads as active-wear rather than hardware. The honest limit: if your commute is a car and a lift lobby, this is not for you.

#### The commute is walked here

Singapore's public transport is excellent, which is exactly why the commute is physical. The train does not come to your door. A typical day includes a walk to the station, a deep interchange, an overhead bridge, a last-mile walk at each end, and often a covered walkway that is longer than it looks. None of it registers as exercise. All of it is charged to the same energy budget as the rest of your evening.

#### Where the 30–50% actually shows up

Not evenly. Assistance concentrates where the cost concentrates:

- Station stairs and overhead bridges — the largest single reduction, because that is where the hip flexors are loaded.
- Long interchange tunnels — a small per-step saving, multiplied by several hundred steps.
- The last mile home — the stretch where fatigue is already accumulated and the saving is felt most.

#### The practical questions people actually ask

Does it fit under a desk — yes, it folds to 2.4 kg. Does it look obvious — it is a slim hip unit worn over clothing and reads as active-wear. Does it survive the rain — IP54, so yes. Does it need charging at work — a 2-hour full charge means one desk session covers the return trip. Does it need an app — no; one button, and posture detection handles the rest.

#### Who this is honestly not for

If you drive door-to-door, or your commute is a lift lobby and a carpark, the assistance has nothing to act on. The same is true of a short flat walk with no stairs. This use case earns its keep on stair-heavy, distance-heavy days — and it is worth being clear about that before a fitting rather than after.

FAQ:

- Q: Can I wear it under office clothing?
  A: It is designed to be worn over clothing at the waist. Most commuters put it on for the walk and stow it at the desk rather than wearing it all day.
- Q: Is it allowed on the MRT?
  A: It is a worn mobility device, not a personal mobility device (PMD) — it has no wheels and no motorised travel. Folded, it is a 2.4 kg item of luggage. If in doubt about a specific operator's policy, check with them directly.
- Q: Will people notice I'm wearing it?
  A: Some will. It is a slim hip belt with short thigh links worn over clothing; most people read it as sports or back-support gear rather than a medical device.

### Trekking poles vs a powered exoskeleton: where the effort goes

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/trekking-poles-vs-powered-exoskeleton/

Question: Are trekking poles or a powered exoskeleton better for climbing?

Answer: They do different jobs. Poles add balance and take load off the knees on descent, at the cost of occupying both hands and adding arm fatigue on long ascents. A powered hip exoskeleton adds up to 16 Nm at the hip flexors — the muscles that actually drive a climb — cutting climbing energy by up to 35% and extending range 2–3x. For a single easy trail, poles are enough. For sustained ascents, repeat training or a return to the trail after injury, the hip assist compounds.

#### The category oversells the summit and undersells the arithmetic

Almost half of everything published about consumer exoskeletons is adventure imagery — the silhouette on the ridgeline. It is also, measurably, the least persuasive material in the category. What hikers actually want to know is arithmetic: how much energy, over what gradient, for what added weight. So here it is.

#### Where each one intervenes

The honest split:

- Poles — excellent for balance, stream crossings and knee load on descent. They shift effort to shoulders and arms; on a long ascent that is a transfer, not a saving.
- Powered hips — up to 16 Nm delivered inside the flexion window of each stride, targeting the muscles doing the climbing. Up to 35% less climbing energy, 2–3x the range.
- Both together — common. Poles for the descent and the scrambles, hip assist for the ascent.

#### Where it earns its 2.4 kg

Any worn device has to pay for its own weight before it saves you anything. On a flat 3 km boardwalk it roughly breaks even. On sustained gradient — a Bukit Timah summit repeat, a Southern Ridges traverse with the bridge climbs, or a training block for an overseas ascent — the saving compounds every step and the 2.4 kg stops being the conversation.

#### Tropical trails are a sealing problem, not a power problem

Local trails are humid, dusty and prone to sudden rain. IP54 covers dust ingress and splashing water from any direction, which is the actual failure mode on a MacRitchie boardwalk in the afternoon — not torque, not battery.

FAQ:

- Q: Do I still need trekking poles?
  A: Many hikers keep them for descent and balance and add hip assist for the climb. They address different problems, so it is not an either/or.
- Q: Will it fit in a daypack?
  A: Yes — it folds down and weighs 2.4 kg, packing roughly like a light insulating layer.
- Q: Is 4 hours enough for a day hike?
  A: For most local day hikes, yes, since assistance is delivered on demand rather than continuously. Sustained climbing draws harder — plan a charge point for multi-day trips.
- Q: Can I train with it for an overseas climb?
  A: Yes, and many users do — but train unassisted sessions too if the summit attempt itself will be unassisted. Assistance changes the training load, which is the point and also the caveat.

### A physiotherapist's guide to powered hip exoskeletons

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/physiotherapist-guide-powered-hip-exoskeleton/

Question: Should a physiotherapist recommend a powered hip exoskeleton to a client?

Answer: Sometimes, and only as an addition to therapy. A consumer hip exoskeleton such as the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro adds up to 16 Nm of assistance as the hip flexes, which can make stairs, slopes and longer walks less costly for a client who can already stand and walk. It does not provide balance support, does not replace a gait programme and is not a medical device. The useful question is not "does it work?" but "does it get this client walking their real routes more often, safely, between sessions?"

#### What the device actually assists

The US-H-1.0Pro is a hip-only, powered exoskeleton. A belt sits at the pelvis, short links run down the outside of each thigh, and a motor at each hip adds torque in the flexion direction while the wearer walks. The spec sheet gives a peak of 16 Nm. The control system reads the gait continuously and switches profile between level ground, stairs and steeper terrain on its own, so there is nothing for the client to adjust mid-walk. When the wearer sits, posture detection pauses assistance; when they stand, it resumes.

What it does not do matters just as much for clinical reasoning:

- It does not assist the knee or ankle directly.
- It does not provide a static support point, so it is not a balance aid in the way a stick or frame is.
- It does not move a limb that the client cannot move. It adds to voluntary effort; it does not create it.
- It does not record clinical outcome measures.

Think of it as a way to lower the cost of hip flexion during real-world walking, not as a training robot.

#### Which clients it tends to suit

In practice the clients who get most from a hip assist device share three traits. They can stand up and walk independently, with or without a stick. Their limiting factor is effort and fatigue rather than balance. And there is a specific route they have stopped doing, such as the stairs to the flat, the walk to the market or an overhead bridge on the way to the clinic.

That profile includes many older adults who have slowly lost walking distance, and people who have finished a formal rehabilitation block but still tire quickly. The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step and a 2–3× increase in walking range; treat those as manufacturer claims for this model, measured under the manufacturer's own conditions, and expect individual results to vary widely.

#### Where caution, or a no, is the right answer

A client whose main problem is balance, dizziness or freezing is better served by the aids and training you already use. Anyone who cannot weight-bear, has not been cleared to load a recently operated joint, or has skin that breaks down easily at the belt and thigh contact points needs a clinical decision first. Our guide to who a powered hip exoskeleton is not for sets out the common exclusions in plain language that you can share with families.

ExoStride is sold as a consumer mobility-assist device. It is not registered as a medical device, and nothing on this site should be read as a treatment claim. If a client asks whether it will fix a condition, the honest answer is no; it may make walking less tiring while they work on that condition with you.

#### How to fit it into a programme

The most useful role a physiotherapist can play is defining the route and the measure. A guided fitting from the Singapore team sets the assistance level and walks the client's own route with them, but you know what the client should be working on, and what they should not.


- Name one route the client has given up and agree on it as the target.
- Decide whether some sessions or days should stay unassisted, so that assistance does not quietly replace training you want them to do.
- Agree a simple measure that the family can record, such as distance walked, number of rest stops, or flights climbed without stopping.
- Review at two and four weeks, as you would any other home programme.

Our guide to tracking progress in the first month gives a simple log that families can fill in without any equipment.

#### Questions worth asking the seller

Physiotherapists are often the only person in the room who will ask the awkward questions. These are fair ones, and the Singapore team can answer them at a demonstration:

- What exactly is measured to support each performance figure, and under which conditions?
- How is assistance level set, and can it be lowered for a cautious first week?
- What happens if the battery runs out mid-walk? (The unit stops assisting but does not lock the legs.)
- Can a clinician attend the fitting?

You can also compare it against the aids a client already uses in our guide on exoskeletons versus canes, frames and wheelchairs.


- Q: Is ExoStride a medical device?
  A: No. The US-H-1.0Pro is a consumer mobility-assist exoskeleton. It is used without a prescription and does not diagnose or treat any condition. Clinical decisions about loading, gait training and fall risk stay with the client's doctor and physiotherapist.
- Q: Can a physiotherapist attend the fitting?
  A: Yes, and it helps. The fitting is done on the client's own route, and having the treating physiotherapist present means the assistance level and target route can be set with the client's programme in mind.
- Q: Will assistance reduce the training effect of walking?
  A: It removes part of the effort of hip flexion, so the training load changes. Many clients walk more often and further with assistance; if a specific strength goal matters, keep some sessions unassisted and decide the balance with the client.
- Q: Does it help with balance?
  A: Not directly. It reduces fatigue and keeps both hands free for a rail, but it does not provide a fixed support point. If balance is the main limitation, a stick or frame and balance training remain first-line.

### After a hip or knee replacement: where a hip exoskeleton fits

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-after-hip-or-knee-replacement/

Question: Can I use a powered hip exoskeleton after a hip or knee replacement?

Answer: Possibly, but only once your surgeon or physiotherapist has cleared you to bear weight and walk the distances you are aiming for. A powered hip exoskeleton is not part of the early, supervised recovery phase. Where it can help is later: when you are walking independently again but still tire on stairs, slopes or longer routes. It is a consumer mobility-assist device, not a medical device, and it works alongside physiotherapy, never instead of it.

#### The short version for families

Joint replacement recovery is a clinical process with its own timeline, exercises and restrictions, and those come from the surgical team. Nothing about a consumer exoskeleton changes that. The sensible way to think about a powered hip exoskeleton is as a possible later step: something to consider once the formal recovery work is well under way and walking is safe, but everyday routes still feel harder than they should.

If you only take one thing from this guide, take this: ask the surgeon or physiotherapist before the first try, and bring this page if it helps the conversation.

#### Why timing matters

In the early weeks after an operation, the priorities are wound healing, managing swelling and pain, protecting the new joint, and relearning a safe walking pattern with whatever aid the team has prescribed. A hip exoskeleton adds torque at the hip as it flexes. For a newly operated hip, that is a load the surgical team needs to agree to. For a newly operated knee, the hip is not the problem joint, but adding a device to the walking pattern while it is still being retrained is still a decision for the team.

Later, the picture changes. Many people reach a point where they are walking without a frame, the exercises are routine, and the remaining problem is stamina: they can do the walk, but it costs more than it used to and they avoid it. That is where an assist device may have a role.

#### What it can and cannot do for you

What the device does, in plain terms:

- It adds up to 16 Nm of assistance at the hip as you lift each leg (spec-sheet figure).
- It reads your gait and adjusts on its own between level ground, stairs and slopes.
- It pauses when you sit down and resumes when you stand.
- The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step and up to 35% less energy on climbs for this model. Those are manufacturer claims; your own result depends on your body, your route and the assistance level.

What it does not do:

- It does not speed up healing or treat the joint.
- It does not replace the strengthening exercises your physiotherapist prescribes.
- It is not a balance aid. If you still need a stick for stability, keep the stick.
- It does not assist the knee directly. After a knee replacement, any benefit comes from making hip flexion cheaper, not from supporting the knee.

#### Questions to clear with your surgical team

Take these to your next review. They are written so you can read them out as they are.

- Am I cleared to bear full weight and walk without restriction on distance?
- Are there any movements or ranges I should still avoid at the hip?
- Is there any reason a belt at the pelvis and straps on the outer thigh would be a problem for my wound or skin?
- Would you prefer that some of my walking stays unassisted, for strength?
- Who should I tell if something feels wrong while using it?

If the answer to the first question is not yet, wait. There is no benefit in rushing.


#### What a sensible first month looks like

Once you are cleared, the Singapore team can do a guided fitting at home or on your own route. The assistance level is set conservatively at first. A pattern that works for many people:

- Week 1: short level walks indoors or along the corridor, 10 to 15 minutes, to get used to the feel.
- Week 2: one flight of stairs, a ramp or a gentle slope, with the handrail.
- Weeks 3 and 4: the route you most want back, such as the market, the park or the bus stop.

Keep your physiotherapy exercises going throughout. Write down how far you walked and how you felt, so you have something concrete to show at your next review. Our guide to fear of falling and walking confidence covers the other half of recovery that rarely gets discussed: the nerves that stay after the joint has healed.

#### For the physiotherapist reading this

If a patient hands you this page, the device is a hip-only, powered flexion assist with automatic terrain switching, no balance function, and a peak of 16 Nm. Our guide for physiotherapists covers suitability, exclusions and how to set a measurable target route.


- Q: How soon after surgery can I try it?
  A: There is no product rule for this; it is a clinical decision. Ask your surgeon or physiotherapist, and wait until you are cleared to bear weight and walk independently on the routes you want to use it for.
- Q: Is it safe to wear over a healing scar?
  A: The belt sits at the pelvis and the links run along the outer thigh. Whether that contact is a problem for your wound depends on where your incision is and how it is healing. Ask your surgical team before wearing it.
- Q: Will it help me stop using my walking stick?
  A: Not necessarily. A stick provides a support point for balance, which the exoskeleton does not. Some people use both. Whether you can stop using the stick is a question for your physiotherapist.
- Q: Can I try it before deciding?
  A: Yes. Fittings in Singapore are done on your own route, so you can feel the assistance on the stairs or slope that matters to you before making any decision.

### How to put on a hip exoskeleton seated: a calm routine

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/how-to-put-on-a-hip-exoskeleton/

Question: How do you put on a powered hip exoskeleton if you have limited mobility?

Answer: Sitting down, in the same chair every time. With the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro the routine is: sit with feet flat, place the belt around the waist and fasten it, settle the thigh straps on the outside of each thigh, check that nothing pinches, then stand with support before pressing the one button. After a fitting, most users can do it seated in under a minute. Nothing requires standing on one leg or bending to the floor.

#### Why a routine matters more than speed

For someone with stiff hips, a sore back or uncertain balance, the hardest part of any walking aid is often not the walk. It is getting ready. Bending to fasten shoes, standing on one leg to step into something, or fiddling with a strap behind the back are all moments where people give up, or fall. A walking aid that is awkward to put on gets left by the door.

A powered hip exoskeleton is worn at the waist and along the outside of the thighs, over normal clothing. That makes it easier than most braces, because nothing goes over the feet. But a good routine still makes the difference between using it every day and using it twice.

#### Before the first time: set up the spot

Choose one chair and keep the device next to it. A firm dining chair with arms is ideal: high enough that standing up is easy, with armrests to push from. Avoid low sofas and soft beds.

- Keep the chair in a well-lit place with a clear path to the door.
- Store the exoskeleton folded on a low shelf or stool beside the chair, not on the floor.
- Put the charger within reach of the same spot, so charging becomes part of taking it off.

Our home set-up checklist covers flooring, charging and storage in more detail.

#### Putting it on, step by step

The exact buckles and adjustments are shown at the fitting, and the team sets the strap lengths so that later you only need to fasten, not adjust. The order below is the general pattern.

- Sit right back in the chair with both feet flat on the floor and knees roughly level with the hips.
- Unfold the device on your lap so the belt faces you and the thigh links hang down on each side.
- Bring the belt around your waist and fasten it at the front. It should sit low, on the bony part of the pelvis, snug but not tight enough to restrict breathing.
- Lay each thigh link along the outside of the thigh and close the thigh strap. You should be able to slide two fingers under it.
- Check for pinching at the waist and the thighs, and that clothing is not bunched underneath.
- Place both hands on the armrests and stand up the way you normally would. If you use a stick or a frame, have it ready.
- Once you are standing steadily, press the one button to start assistance.

After a fitting, the manufacturer says most users can do this seated in under a minute. In the first week, give it five. Rushing is how straps end up twisted.


#### Sitting down and getting up again

You do not need to switch the device off to sit. Posture detection pauses assistance when you sit and resumes it when you stand, so a rest on a bench or at the kopitiam does not need any action. If you are going to sit for a long time, switching off saves battery.

#### Taking it off

- Sit down in your chair first.
- Switch the device off.
- Open the thigh straps, then the belt.
- Fold it on your lap and put it back on its shelf.
- Plug in the charger if you will use it again tomorrow. A full charge takes two hours.

#### When a family member helps

If a son, daughter, spouse or helper assists, agree who does what. A good split is that the wearer fastens the belt themselves and the helper closes the thigh straps. That keeps the wearer in charge, which matters more than it sounds. Our caregiver's guide covers how to raise the idea without it feeling like a judgement.

#### Signs the fit needs adjusting

- Red marks that are still visible twenty minutes after taking it off.
- The belt slides up towards the ribs as you walk.
- The thigh links rotate to the front of the leg.
- You feel the assistance pushing at a moment that feels wrong.

Any of these is a reason to contact the team rather than live with it. See our guide to how a hip exoskeleton should fit for what good looks like.


- Q: Do I need to stand to put it on?
  A: No. The whole routine is done seated, and you only stand once the belt and thigh straps are fastened. Start the assistance after you are standing steadily.
- Q: Can I wear it over a sarong, skirt or dress?
  A: It is designed to be worn over clothing at the waist and thighs. Loose or long fabric can bunch under the straps, so try your usual clothing at the fitting and the team will advise.
- Q: What if my hands are weak or arthritic?
  A: Raise it at the fitting. The team sets strap lengths in advance so that daily use is mostly fastening, and a family member or helper can do the thigh straps.
- Q: Does it need an app to start?
  A: No. One button starts assistance. The app is optional and is only used for settings.

### Fear of falling: rebuilding walking confidence after a fall

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/fear-of-falling-walking-confidence/

Question: How do you rebuild walking confidence after a fall?

Answer: Gradually, on routes that matter, with the actual cause of the fall dealt with first. Start with a check-up with a doctor or physiotherapist, fix what made the fall likely, then rebuild short, successful walks before longer ones. A powered hip exoskeleton can help when tiredness is part of the problem, because it takes some of the effort out of stairs and longer walks. It does not stop falls and is not a balance aid; if balance is the main issue, a stick, frame and balance training come first.

#### The fall is one event. The fear can last for years.

A fall often heals faster than the confidence it takes away. Bruises fade in a fortnight; the habit of avoiding the stairs, skipping the market and staying in the chair can settle in for good. Families notice it as a quiet shrinking of routine: fewer outings, shorter walks, more "I'll go tomorrow".

The difficult part is that avoiding walking is understandable and also makes things worse. Less walking means less strength and stamina, which makes the next walk harder and more tiring, which makes a stumble more likely. Breaking that loop is the real goal, and it is mostly about small, successful walks rather than equipment.

#### Step one: find out why the fall happened

Before anything is bought, the person who fell should see a doctor. Falls in older adults can have many causes, and some of them are treatable: eyesight, blood pressure on standing, medication side effects, foot problems, or a home hazard such as a loose mat. A physiotherapist can assess strength and balance and suggest the right aid.

This guide does not replace that check. It is about what comes after.

#### Step two: separate balance from tiredness

It helps to ask honestly which of these describes the fall:

- Balance: a wobble or loss of footing, often at a turn, a kerb or when standing up.
- Tiredness: legs that felt heavy, a foot that did not lift high enough on a step, a stumble near the end of a long walk.
- Environment: a wet floor, poor light, an uneven surface.

Different answers lead to different help. For balance, the established tools are a walking stick or frame, balance exercises and sometimes a home assessment. For environment, it is lighting, rails and removing trip hazards. For tiredness, the options are building stamina gradually and, for some people, reducing the effort each step costs. That last one is where a powered hip exoskeleton can play a part.

#### Where a hip exoskeleton fits, honestly

The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro adds assistance at the hip as each leg lifts, with a peak of 16 Nm on the spec sheet. The manufacturer claims it reduces lower-body load per step by up to 80% and extends walking range by two to three times. Treat those as manufacturer claims; your own experience will depend on your body and your route.

What this can mean in daily life is that the last flight of stairs, or the last stretch home from the market, costs less. Feet that drag when tired may lift more easily on steps. And because nothing is held in the hands, both hands stay free for a handrail.


What it cannot do is just as important:

- It does not catch you or stop a fall.
- It does not give you a fixed support point the way a stick or frame does.
- It does not fix dizziness, poor eyesight or a medication problem.

If the honest answer to step two was balance, start with the aids and training your physiotherapist recommends. Our comparison of exoskeletons, canes, frames and wheelchairs shows what each one restores.

#### Step three: rebuild with small wins

Confidence returns through experience, not reassurance. A simple plan:

- Pick one route that was given up, such as the corridor to the lift, the walk to the bus stop or one flight of stairs.
- Walk it at the best time of day, usually mid-morning, with someone alongside at first.
- Keep it short enough to finish feeling fine, not exhausted.
- Repeat it until it feels ordinary, then extend it by one stop, one block or one flight.
- Write down each walk. Seeing the list grow is more convincing than any encouragement.

Our guide to keeping a daily walking routine in Singapore has practical ideas for timing walks around the heat and finding routes with places to rest.

#### Talking about it without making it worse

People who are afraid of falling often feel embarrassed about it. "You need to be more careful" tends to land as criticism. "Shall we try the walk to the market together on Saturday?" lands as an invitation. Focus on the place they miss, not the fall.


- Q: Will an exoskeleton stop my parent from falling?
  A: No device can promise that. A powered hip exoskeleton reduces the effort of walking and can help when tiredness contributes to stumbles, but it does not catch a fall or provide a support point. Talk to their doctor or physiotherapist about fall risk.
- Q: Should they stop using their walking stick?
  A: Not because of an exoskeleton. A stick provides balance support, which the exoskeleton does not. Many people use both. Any change to walking aids should be agreed with a physiotherapist.
- Q: What if they are too nervous to try it?
  A: That is common. A single, no-obligation fitting on a short route they already know, with a family member present, is usually the gentlest start.
- Q: Is it heavy to wear?
  A: It weighs 2.4 kg and sits at the waist, so the weight rests on the pelvis rather than the shoulders.

### Keeping a daily walk in your 70s and 80s in Singapore

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/daily-walking-routine-older-adults-singapore/

Question: How can an older adult keep up a daily walk in Singapore?

Answer: Make it short, regular and planned around the climate. Walk early in the morning or in the late afternoon, choose routes with shade, seats and toilets, and build up slowly from a distance that feels easy. Consistency matters more than distance. If stairs, slopes or tiredness are what stop the walk, a powered hip exoskeleton can take some of the effort out of each step. Check with a doctor before starting a new exercise routine, especially after illness or a fall.

#### Why the daily walk is worth protecting

For many older Singaporeans, the daily walk is more than exercise. It is the trip to the market, the coffee shop catch-up, the stroll around the void deck and the reason to get dressed. When it stops, a lot else stops with it. Protecting the walk is protecting independence.

The good news is that a useful routine does not have to be long or strenuous. What matters most is doing something most days.

#### Start with a check, then start small

If you have been unwell, had a fall, have a heart or lung condition, or have not walked regularly for a while, see your doctor before starting. They can tell you whether there is anything to watch for.

Then start with a walk that feels comfortably easy. For some people that is five minutes along the corridor; for others it is a lap of the neighbourhood park. Finish feeling like you could have done a little more. That feeling is what brings you back tomorrow.

#### Plan around the heat

Singapore is hot and humid all year, and older bodies handle heat less well. A few habits make a big difference:

- Walk early, before mid-morning, or in the late afternoon once the sun is lower.
- Choose covered walkways, void decks and tree-lined park paths.
- Carry water and drink before you feel thirsty.
- Wear a hat, light loose clothing and shoes with a good grip.
- On a very hot day, walk indoors instead, such as in a shopping mall or the corridors of your block.

Our guide to walking in Singapore's heat goes into pacing and warning signs in more detail.

#### Choose routes with somewhere to stop

A route with benches every few hundred metres is far more inviting than one without. Good options in most estates include the neighbourhood park, the estate's covered linkways and the nearest park connector. Our guide to park connector walks covers planning longer, flat routes.

Make each walk end somewhere pleasant: a kopitiam, a friend's block, the market. A walk with a destination happens far more reliably than a walk for its own sake.


#### Build distance slowly

A simple way to progress without overdoing it:

- Weeks 1 and 2: the same short route every day, at the same time.
- Weeks 3 and 4: add one extra stretch, such as one more block or one more lap.
- After that: add one longer walk a week, keeping the others short.

Keep a note of each walk. The note is useful for you, and for your doctor or physiotherapist.

#### When stairs and tiredness are the problem

Some people can walk on the flat but avoid routes with stairs, slopes or an overhead bridge. Others manage the first half of a walk and dread the way back. In those cases, reducing the effort of each step can keep the routine going.

The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a powered hip exoskeleton that adds up to 16 Nm of assistance as each leg lifts. The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step and a two- to three-fold increase in walking range for this model; those are manufacturer claims and individual results vary. It weighs 2.4 kg, is worn over clothing, starts with one button and pauses when you sit on a bench.

It is not a substitute for the routine itself, and it is not a balance aid. If you are unsteady rather than tired, a walking stick and balance exercises suggested by a physiotherapist come first. Our guide to fear of falling covers that side.

#### Walking with company

Walking with a friend, a spouse or a walking group makes it much more likely to happen. Many community centres and residents' networks run group walks; ask at yours. If a family member walks with you once a week, make that the longer walk.


- Q: How far should an older adult walk each day?
  A: There is no single right number. It depends on health, fitness and what your doctor advises. Regular, comfortable walks most days are more useful than an occasional long one. Increase gradually.
- Q: Is it safe to walk in the afternoon heat?
  A: Midday and early afternoon are the hardest times for older adults. Walk early or in the late afternoon, stay in the shade, drink water, and stop if you feel dizzy, unwell or unusually breathless.
- Q: Does a hip exoskeleton make the walk too easy to be exercise?
  A: You are still walking on your own legs; it removes part of the effort of lifting each leg. Many people walk further and more often with assistance. If a specific strength goal matters, ask a physiotherapist how to balance assisted and unassisted walks.
- Q: Can I use it on a rainy day?
  A: It is IP54-rated, which covers splashing water from any direction, such as rain while walking. For your own safety, wet surfaces are still slippery.

### Wearing a mobility aid without feeling old

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/wearing-a-mobility-aid-in-public/

Question: How do you get past feeling embarrassed about using a mobility aid?

Answer: By focusing on what the aid gives back rather than what it says about you. Most people refuse a walking aid because of how it looks, not how it works, and the cost is staying home. Choosing an aid that fits your life, practising on familiar routes, and having a short answer ready for curious people all help. A powered hip exoskeleton is worn at the waist over clothing and is often read as sports or back-support gear, which some people find easier to accept than a stick or frame.

#### The aid that stays in the cupboard

Ask any physiotherapist and you will hear the same story. A walking stick is prescribed, bought, and then left behind the door. A frame is used at home but never outside. The reason is rarely that the aid does not work. It is that using it in front of the neighbours feels like announcing that you have become old.

That feeling deserves respect rather than a lecture. It is also worth naming its cost: when the aid stays in the cupboard, the walk often does too.

#### Why it feels the way it does

Visible aids carry strong associations. A stick or a frame says "frail" to many people of our parents' generation, and nobody wants to be seen that way by the uncle at the coffee shop or the aunties at the market. Pride is also wrapped up with independence: accepting help with walking can feel like the first step towards needing help with everything.

Understanding this helps families too. Arguing about safety statistics rarely works. Talking about what the person wants to keep doing usually does.

#### Reframe the aid around what it gives back

People accept tools that let them do things. Very few people feel embarrassed about reading glasses, because glasses mean reading. The same shift works for walking aids:

- Not "you need a stick", but "this means you can do the market on your own again".
- Not "you are not safe", but "this would make the stairs to your friend's flat easier".
- Not "everyone your age uses one", but "try it once on the walk you miss".

#### Where a hip exoskeleton reads differently

A powered hip exoskeleton such as the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a slim belt at the waist with short links along the outside of each thigh, worn over clothing. Nothing is held in the hands. Many people who see it assume it is sports equipment or a back support. Some wearers like that it looks like technology rather than infirmity.

It is not invisible, and it is not for everyone. It does a different job from a stick or frame: it takes some of the effort out of lifting each leg, with a peak of 16 Nm on the spec sheet, rather than giving you something to lean on. If balance is the main problem, a stick or frame is still the right tool, and the pride question has to be faced directly. Our comparison of mobility aids explains which problem each one solves.


#### Practise where nobody is watching

The first outing with any new aid is the hardest. Make it easy:

- Start at home and in the corridor, where nobody you know will pass.
- Next, try a quiet time at a familiar place, such as the park early in the morning.
- Then the real target: the market, the temple, the bus stop.

The Singapore team fits the exoskeleton at home or on your own route, so the first try can be private.

#### Have a one-line answer ready

Curious people will ask. A short, cheerful answer ends the conversation on your terms:

- "It's a walking assist. Makes the stairs easier."
- "It's like an e-bike for walking."
- "My grandson made me get it. It's actually quite good."

Most people ask because they are interested, and many ask because they are thinking about a parent of their own.

#### For families raising the subject

If you are the son, daughter or spouse, let the person choose. Offer a trial rather than a purchase, attach it to a place they miss, and do not make it a conversation about decline. Our caregiver's guide has more on how to raise it without it landing as an insult, and our guide to keeping up with the grandchildren is about the moments that often matter most.

#### Small things that make it easier

- Wear it with clothes you feel good in; a favourite shirt helps more than you would think.
- Go out with someone the first few times, so you can chat instead of thinking about it.
- Choose a destination you enjoy, not just a walk for its own sake.
- Notice how many other people use aids of all kinds. You are rarely the only one.


- Q: Will people notice that I am wearing it?
  A: Some will. It is a slim hip belt with short thigh links worn over clothing. Most people read it as sports or back-support gear rather than a medical device.
- Q: Can I wear it under clothes to hide it?
  A: It is designed to be worn over clothing at the waist. A loose shirt or light jacket over the belt makes it less noticeable.
- Q: Is it a medical device?
  A: No. It is a consumer mobility-assist device. It does not need a prescription and does not diagnose or treat any condition.
- Q: Can I try it somewhere private first?
  A: Yes. Fittings are done at home or on your own route, so the first walk can be somewhere nobody is watching.

### Who a powered hip exoskeleton is not for: an honest checklist

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/who-should-not-use-powered-hip-exoskeleton/

Question: Who should not use a powered hip exoskeleton?

Answer: People who cannot stand and walk on their own, people whose main problem is balance rather than effort, and anyone with a recent operation, injury or condition that a doctor has not cleared for walking with added hip assistance. Skin that breaks down easily at the waist or thighs, and devices or conditions that a doctor has flagged, also need a medical opinion first. A powered hip exoskeleton assists walking you can already do; it does not replace a wheelchair, a frame or medical care.

#### Why we wrote a guide about who should not buy

The fastest way to waste money on mobility equipment is to buy the right product for the wrong problem. A powered hip exoskeleton solves one problem well: walking that is possible but too tiring, especially on stairs, slopes and longer routes. For other problems it is the wrong tool, and an honest seller should say so before a fitting, not after.

This page is general information, not medical advice. If anything below applies to you or your parent, talk to a doctor or physiotherapist first.

#### The three questions to answer first

- Can the person stand up and walk on their own, with or without a stick? If not, a hip exoskeleton is not the right starting point.
- Is the main problem effort or balance? Heavy legs, running out of energy and avoiding stairs point to effort. Wobbling, near-falls and needing to hold on point to balance.
- Is there anything a doctor has said about walking, exercise or the hips that has not been checked against using an assist device?

If the answers are yes, effort and no, an exoskeleton may be worth a trial. Otherwise, read on.

#### When it is the wrong tool

- Unable to stand or walk independently. The device adds to the movement you make; it does not create movement. A wheelchair, transfer aid or supervised rehabilitation is the right category.
- Balance as the main limitation. The exoskeleton does not provide a support point to lean on. A stick, frame and balance training are first-line. Our comparison of mobility aids explains the difference.
- Severe breathlessness or chest pain on walking. Reducing the leg effort does not address the reason walking is hard. See a doctor.
- Pain that is the main reason for not walking. If walking hurts, the cause needs to be assessed, not worked around.

#### When to get a doctor's go-ahead first

These are not automatic exclusions, but they need a medical opinion before the first try:

- A recent operation on the hip, knee, spine or abdomen, or any surgery where you have been told to limit movement or loading. Our guide to life after a joint replacement covers this in detail.
- A recent fracture or significant injury of the leg, pelvis or spine.
- Skin that is fragile, broken or slow to heal where the belt and thigh straps sit.
- Significant swelling of the legs, or circulation problems where straps could be a concern.
- Any implanted medical device, or a condition where your doctor has advised caution with electronic or motorised equipment worn on the body.
- Pregnancy, because the belt sits around the pelvis.
- Conditions affecting judgement or memory, where the wearer may not be able to say if something is uncomfortable.


#### When it may be fine, but not the best value

Some people can use the device perfectly well but will not get much from it. If you walk long distances comfortably, climb stairs without thinking about it and are not trying to extend your range, the assistance may feel pleasant but unnecessary. Equally, if every journey you make is by car door to door, there may be too little walking for it to matter.

#### What we suggest instead of guessing

If you are unsure, show this page to the person's doctor or physiotherapist. Our guide for physiotherapists explains what the device assists in clinical terms. And remember that a fitting with the Singapore team is a trial on your own route, not a commitment. If it does not suit, it is far better to find out on the stairs at home than after a purchase.

#### If it is a no for now

A no is not always permanent. Someone recovering from surgery may become a good candidate once they are cleared and walking independently. Someone whose balance improves with training may find that effort becomes the limiting factor later. And a person for whom a hip exoskeleton is the wrong tool may still benefit from the right one: a stick, a frame, a rollator, home modifications or a physiotherapy programme. The aim is the same in every case: walking the routes that matter, safely.


- Q: Do I need a prescription to buy one?
  A: No. The US-H-1.0Pro is a consumer mobility-assist device and does not need a prescription. That is exactly why it is worth checking suitability with a doctor or physiotherapist yourself when any of the points above apply.
- Q: My parent uses a walking frame. Can they switch to an exoskeleton?
  A: Not as a straight swap. A frame provides support for balance; the exoskeleton reduces effort. Some people use both. Ask their physiotherapist before changing aids.
- Q: Is there a weight or height limit?
  A: Fit depends on waist and thigh measurements and on the configuration supplied. Ask the Singapore team before booking, and the fitting will confirm it.
- Q: What if we try it and it does not suit?
  A: That is what the fitting is for. It is done on your own route, so you will know whether it helps before deciding anything.

### Is it working? What to track in the first month with an exoskeleton

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/tracking-progress-with-a-powered-exoskeleton/

Question: How do you know if a powered exoskeleton is actually helping?

Answer: Track the same few things before and after: one route you care about, how far you walked, how many times you stopped to rest, how many flights of stairs you managed, and how tired you felt afterwards on a 0 to 10 scale. Write them down for a week without the device, then for four weeks with it. If the route gets easier, longer or more frequent, it is helping you. If nothing changes after a month, talk to the team and your physiotherapist rather than persisting.

#### Why your own numbers matter more than ours

Every exoskeleton brand publishes performance figures. For the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro, the manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step, up to 35% less energy on climbs and two to three times the walking range. Those are manufacturer claims, measured under the manufacturer's conditions. They are a reason to try the device, not a prediction of what it will do for you.

What actually matters is simple: does the person walk more, more comfortably, on the routes they care about? You can answer that without any equipment, as long as you write things down.

#### The five things to record

Use a notebook, a calendar on the fridge or a note on a phone. After each walk, record:

- The route: the same named route each time, such as "home to market and back".
- Distance or time: either works, as long as you are consistent. A phone step counter is fine if you already use one.
- Rest stops: how many times you stopped to sit or lean.
- Stairs: how many flights climbed without stopping.
- Effort: how tiring it felt afterwards, on a scale from 0 (no effort) to 10 (the hardest possible).

Add one line of comments if something stood out, such as "very hot", "slept badly" or "walked with a friend".

#### First, a baseline week without the device

If you can, record a normal week before the device arrives. Without a baseline, it is hard to tell whether a good day is down to the assistance or the weather. If a week is not possible, record two or three walks of the main route, unassisted, with someone alongside.

#### The first four weeks

Keep the route the same for the first fortnight so the comparison is fair. A sensible pattern, which the fitting team will adjust to the person:

- Week 1: get used to the feel. Expect your records to be similar to the baseline, or a little better.
- Week 2: the same route, with the assistance level the fitting team set. This is where changes in rest stops and effort usually show.
- Weeks 3 and 4: extend the route by one stretch, or add a route that had been given up.


#### What progress looks like

Progress is not always a bigger number. Any of these is a good sign:

- Fewer rest stops on the same route.
- A lower effort score for the same walk.
- The same walk done on more days of the week.
- A route that had been given up, done again.
- Less tiredness the evening after a walk.

If the effort score drops but distance does not change, that still counts. Many people care more about arriving home with energy left than about walking further.

#### When to adjust, and when to stop

- If effort scores go up, or new aches appear, stop and contact the team. Fit and assistance level can often be adjusted.
- If nothing changes after four weeks of regular use, raise it honestly with the team and with a physiotherapist. The device may not suit the problem. Our guide to who a hip exoskeleton is not for covers the common reasons.
- If there is pain, dizziness, a fall or a near-fall, stop and see a doctor.

#### Share the log

A written log is the most useful thing to bring to a physiotherapy appointment. It turns "I think it's better" into evidence. Our guide for physiotherapists suggests how the treating physio can set the target route. And if you want to understand how researchers measure the same things in a lab, see our guide to judging exoskeleton performance claims.

#### A sample week of entries

- Mon: home to market and back, 25 min, 2 rest stops, 1 flight, effort 6.
- Wed: same route, 24 min, 2 rest stops, 1 flight, effort 5, hot.
- Fri: same route, 23 min, 1 rest stop, 2 flights, effort 5.
- Sun: park loop with family, 35 min, 2 rest stops, 0 flights, effort 4.

Four lines a week is enough to see a trend.


- Q: Do I need a fitness tracker or smartwatch?
  A: No. A notebook works. If you already use a phone step counter or watch, it can help with distance, but rest stops, stairs and how it felt are just as important and need only a pen.
- Q: How long before I should notice a difference?
  A: Some people feel the assistance immediately on stairs. Changes in routine and stamina take longer, which is why a fair judgement needs about four weeks of regular use.
- Q: Should I compare my results with the manufacturer's figures?
  A: Not directly. The manufacturer's figures are claims measured under specific conditions. Your own log on your own route is the better test of whether it helps you.
- Q: Can the app track this for me?
  A: The app is optional and used for settings. Walking never requires it. A simple written log is the most reliable record and easy to share with a physiotherapist.

### Keeping up with the grandchildren: school runs and playgrounds

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/keeping-up-with-grandchildren-mobility/

Question: How can grandparents with tired legs keep up with active grandchildren?

Answer: Plan outings around rest points, keep both hands free, and reduce the effort of the parts that tire you most: stairs, overhead bridges and the walk home. Many Singapore grandparents do the school run and the playground daily. If effort rather than balance is what slows you down, a powered hip exoskeleton can take some of the work out of each step. It is worn at the waist, leaves both hands free for small hands, and pauses when you sit on the bench.

#### The most demanding job of retirement

In many Singapore families, grandparents are the after-school plan. The day might include a walk to the bus stop, the school gate, an overhead bridge, the playground, the market for dinner and back up to the flat, often carrying a school bag. It is a lot of walking for anyone, and more so for knees and hips in their seventies.

Grandparents rarely complain about it. More often they quietly cut things out: the playground becomes the void deck, the outing to the park becomes the television. This guide is about keeping the good parts.

#### Plan the outing around rest points

Children run; grandparents do not need to. Choose outings where you can sit while the children play:

- Playgrounds with shaded benches facing the play area.
- Parks with a loop path, so the children can lap you while you walk at your own pace.
- Malls on hot or rainy days, with lifts, seating and toilets.

Before a longer outing, think through the return journey. Most people tire on the way home, not the way out.

#### Keep both hands free

A child's hand in one hand and a school bag in the other leaves nothing for the handrail. Small changes help:

- Use a backpack for the school bag and the water bottles.
- Teach older grandchildren to hold the handrail on stairs themselves.
- Leave the umbrella in the bag unless it is raining.

Any walking aid that needs a hand has a cost here. A stick competes with a small hand. This is one place where a hands-free aid has a real advantage.

#### Where a powered hip exoskeleton can help

The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a slim belt at the waist with short links on the outside of each thigh, worn over clothing. It adds up to 16 Nm of assistance as each leg lifts (spec-sheet figure), adjusts automatically for stairs and slopes, and pauses when you sit on the playground bench. The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step and up to 35% less energy on climbs; those are manufacturer claims, and what you feel will depend on you and your route.


In practice, grandparents tend to notice it on:

- The overhead bridge on the way to school.
- The stairs at the MRT station or the playground.
- The walk home at the end of the afternoon, when legs are heaviest.

It runs for up to 4 hours of assistance per charge and charges fully in two hours, which covers a typical afternoon. Our guide to battery life explains how stairs and slopes affect that.

#### What it is not

It is not a balance aid, and it will not catch you if a child pulls you off balance. If you are unsteady, a physiotherapist can advise on the right aid and exercises. It is also not something children should play with; fold it away out of reach when you take it off.

#### The pride question

Some grandparents worry that wearing a mobility aid in front of the grandchildren, or the other parents at the school gate, will make them look frail. Children are usually more curious than anything else, and some will simply think it looks like a robot suit. Our guide to wearing a mobility aid in public has practical ideas for the adults.

#### For the parents reading this

If your parents look after your children, the outings they quietly drop are a sign. Ask which part of the day is hardest. If it is stairs or the walk home, a trial fitting on that exact route is a practical, low-pressure way to find out whether hip assistance helps.

#### A sample school-run afternoon

A realistic plan for a grandparent doing the afternoon pick-up:

- Charge the device in the morning and put it on after lunch, seated.
- Walk to school using the route with the fewest stairs, even if it is a little longer.
- Sit on a shaded bench at the playground while the children play; assistance pauses on its own.
- Walk home before the children are tired, so nobody needs carrying.
- Take the device off in your usual chair and put it back on charge.


- Q: Can I carry a child while wearing it?
  A: The device assists your walking; it does not support extra weight. Lifting and carrying a child adds load, so be careful on stairs and use the handrail. Talk to your doctor if lifting is a concern.
- Q: Will the battery last a whole afternoon?
  A: Up to 4 hours of assistance per charge, according to the spec sheet. Assistance is delivered as you walk, and stair-heavy routes draw more, so charge it fully before a long outing.
- Q: Can I sit on the playground bench with it on?
  A: Yes. Posture detection pauses assistance when you sit and resumes when you stand, so there is nothing to switch.
- Q: Is it safe around young children?
  A: Treat it like any electrical device: fold it away out of reach when you are not wearing it, and keep small fingers away from the hip joints while you are walking.

### Walking together again: pacing outings with an older parent

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/walking-together-caregiver-and-parent/

Question: How do you plan a walk with an elderly parent who tires easily?

Answer: Let them set the pace, plan the route backwards from the way home, and build in a rest stop before they need one. Choose shade, seats and toilets, walk early or late in the day, and watch for quiet signs of tiredness such as shorter steps, a dragging foot or going silent. If effort on stairs and slopes is what limits the outing, a powered hip exoskeleton can reduce the work of each step; if balance is the issue, ask a physiotherapist about the right aid.

#### The outing that used to be easy

There is a moment many adult children recognise. The Sunday walk around the reservoir, the trip to the temple or the family dinner across town starts to end early. A parent who used to stride ahead now says "you go, I'll wait here". Nobody decides to stop going out together; it just happens, one shortened outing at a time.

This guide is about getting those outings back, with your parent still in charge of them.

#### Let them set the pace

The single biggest change is also the simplest: walk at their speed, not yours. Adults walking with an older parent often slow down without realising they are still pulling slightly ahead. That creates pressure to keep up, which is tiring and can lead to rushed, careless steps.

- Walk beside them, not in front.
- If you are pushing a pram or carrying bags, let them lead.
- Stop when they stop, without comment.

#### Plan the route backwards

Most people tire on the way back. Plan the outing from the return journey:

- Where is the nearest taxi stand or bus stop to the furthest point?
- Is there a route home with fewer stairs, even if it is longer?
