- Where are the seats, toilets and shade?

A loop with a café or bench at the halfway point works better than an out-and-back walk to a distant destination.

#### Rest before it is needed

Build in a sit-down at regular intervals, and take it whether or not your parent asks. Many older people will not ask for a rest because they do not want to slow the family down. Making it part of the plan removes the awkwardness.

#### Watch for the quiet signs

People rarely say "I'm exhausted". Watch instead for:

- Shorter steps, or a foot that scuffs the ground.
- Holding on to railings or walls more than usual.
- Going quiet, or becoming irritable.
- Asking how much further it is.

When you see these, find a seat. Pushing on is when stumbles happen.


#### Mind the heat

Singapore's heat and humidity are hard on older bodies. Walk in the early morning or late afternoon, carry water for both of you, and choose covered walkways and shaded paths. On very hot days, a mall walk is a perfectly good outing. Our guide to walking in Singapore heat has more on pacing.

#### When effort is the limit

If your parent can walk but runs out of energy, especially on stairs, slopes and overhead bridges, reducing the effort of each step can extend the outing. The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a powered hip exoskeleton worn over clothing at the waist. It adds up to 16 Nm of assistance as each leg lifts (spec-sheet figure), adjusts on its own for stairs and slopes, and pauses when they sit down. The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step and two to three times the walking range; those are manufacturer claims, and individual results vary.

Because nothing is held in the hands, your parent can hold your arm or a handrail. That matters on stairs.

If balance rather than effort is the issue, a stick or frame recommended by a physiotherapist is the better tool. Our caregiver's guide covers how to choose and how to raise the subject.

#### Do not take over

The aim is a shared walk, not a supervised one. Avoid narrating every kerb, holding their arm without being asked, or deciding for them when the walk is over. Ask. Most parents will tell you more about how they feel if they do not feel managed.

#### A sample Sunday outing

- Choose a loop in a park near a taxi stand or bus stop, with a café or bench at the halfway point.
- Leave early, before the heat builds.
- Walk side by side at your parent's pace and stop at the halfway point whether or not they ask.
- Decide together whether to finish the loop or head straight home.
- Keep a note of how far you went, so next week can be a little longer if they want.


- Q: My parent insists they are fine but always stops early. What should I do?
  A: Plan the rest stops in advance so they do not have to ask. Choose shorter loops with a pleasant halfway point. If they still tire quickly, a check with their doctor is worth it.
- Q: Should I hold my parent's arm while walking?
  A: Offer, do not insist. Some people find it reassuring, others feel patronised. On stairs, a handrail is usually more stable than another person's arm.
- Q: Can a hip exoskeleton replace the walking stick on outings?
  A: Not if the stick is for balance. The exoskeleton reduces effort but does not provide a support point. Many people use both; ask a physiotherapist.
- Q: How long does the battery last on a family day out?
  A: Up to 4 hours of assistance per charge on the spec sheet, with a full charge in two hours. Stairs and slopes use more, so charge it fully before a long outing.

### Getting the home ready for a powered exoskeleton: a checklist

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-home-setup-checklist/

Question: How should you prepare a home for a powered hip exoskeleton?

Answer: Pick one sturdy chair with armrests as the dressing spot, store the folded device beside it rather than on the floor, put the charger within reach of the same spot, and clear trip hazards on the routes it will be used on. The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is 2.4 kg and folds, so it needs no special storage, but a fixed routine around one spot makes daily use far more likely. Basic fall-prevention steps at home still apply.

#### Why the home set-up decides whether it gets used

Most mobility aids fail not on the walk but at the door. If a device lives in a cupboard, needs hunting for the charger, or has to be put on standing up in a narrow corridor, it gets used less and less. A small amount of planning before the device arrives turns it into part of the daily routine instead of a project.

Everything below can be done in an afternoon, and most of it is useful whether or not you end up using an exoskeleton.

#### Choose the dressing spot

Pick one chair and use it every time.

- Firm, stable and with armrests to push up from.
- Seat height so that the knees are roughly level with the hips when the feet are flat.
- Not on wheels, and not a low sofa or the edge of a soft bed.
- Near the main door, so the device goes on as part of leaving the flat.
- With enough clear space in front to stand up and take the first steps.

Our step-by-step guide to putting on a hip exoskeleton seated is built around this chair.

#### Storage

The US-H-1.0Pro weighs 2.4 kg and folds. Store it:

- Folded, on a low shelf, stool or side table next to the dressing chair, at a height that needs no bending to the floor.
- Out of reach of small children and pets.
- Away from direct sunlight and not in a car boot, since sustained heat is bad for any lithium battery.
- Somewhere dry. It is IP54-rated against dust and splashing water, but it should not sit in a wet bathroom.

#### Charging

A full charge takes two hours, and the spec sheet gives up to 4 hours of assistance per charge. The simplest habit is to charge it every time it comes off.

- Put the charger at a socket beside the dressing spot, so charging needs no walking or bending.
- Route the cable along the wall, never across a walkway.
- Choose a socket that is easy to reach without kneeling.
- If an older person will charge it themselves, show them once and leave a simple written note by the socket.

Our guide to battery life explains how terrain affects how long a charge lasts.


#### Clear the routes it will be used on

An exoskeleton helps with effort; it does nothing for a loose mat. Walk the routes the person uses most, at home and just outside, and look for:

- Loose rugs and mats, especially at the bathroom and kitchen doors.
- Cables and clutter on the floor.
- Poor lighting in the corridor and at the main door, including at night.
- Shoe racks and pots that narrow the corridor outside the flat.
- Steps or a raised threshold at the main door or the bathroom that are easy to miss.

Grab bars in the bathroom and good lighting are worth having anyway. For a broader view of staying independent at home, read our guide to aging in place with a powered exoskeleton.

#### Plan the first routes

Before the fitting, decide which one or two routes matter most, such as the corridor to the lift, the stairs to the next floor, the walk to the market or the bus stop. The fitting team will walk them with the user, so it helps if they are agreed in advance.

#### Who will help, and when

If a family member or helper will assist with putting it on, charging or the first walks, agree it in advance and make sure they attend the fitting. One person who knows how everything works makes a big difference in the first fortnight.

#### The first week at home

Keep the first week simple. Use the same chair, the same time of day and the same short route, so the routine forms before the walks get longer. Put a small note by the chair with the order of steps from the fitting, and another by the charger. If anything is awkward, such as a strap that is hard to reach or a cable in the way, change the set-up rather than working around it. Small frictions in the first week are what decide whether the device is still being used a month later.


- Q: Where is the best place for the charger?
  A: Next to the dressing chair, at a socket you can reach without kneeling, with the cable running along the wall rather than across the floor. Charging then becomes part of taking it off.
- Q: Can it be stored in the bathroom or kitchen?
  A: It is better kept in a dry room. IP54 covers dust and splashing water, but a humid bathroom is not ideal storage for electronics.
- Q: Do we need to change anything at the HDB block?
  A: No changes are needed to use it. Stairs and slopes are where the assistance is most noticeable. It is still worth noting which routes have handrails.
- Q: Does the fitting happen at home?
  A: Yes. A team member brings the unit, sizes it, sets the assistance level and walks the chosen route with the user.

### How to read an exoskeleton spec sheet: the numbers that matter

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/how-to-read-an-exoskeleton-spec-sheet/

Question: What should you look for on an exoskeleton spec sheet?

Answer: Seven lines matter most: which joint it assists, peak torque, total weight and where it sits, assistance time per charge, charge time, ingress (IP) rating and how it is controlled. Read each in context: torque only matters if it is well timed, battery hours depend on terrain, and weight matters less than where it rests. Performance percentages are a separate category; they are manufacturer claims and should be read as "up to", under the maker's test conditions. For the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro: hip, 16 Nm, 2.4 kg, up to 4 h, 2 h, IP54, one button.

#### Why spec sheets are hard to compare

Exoskeleton makers do not publish their specifications in the same format. One lists torque per joint, another lists combined torque. One quotes battery life in hours, another in kilometres. Some list weight without the battery. Performance percentages sit right next to measured specifications as if they were the same kind of number. They are not.

This guide goes through a spec sheet line by line, using the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro as the worked example, and says what each line tells you and what it does not.

#### 1. Which joint is assisted

This is the most important line and often the least prominent. Exoskeletons for walking typically assist the hip, the knee, the ankle, or several joints. Each changes a different part of the step. Hip devices help lift the leg, which is where much of the effort of stairs and slopes goes. Knee devices tend to focus on support and the knee's extension. Ankle devices assist push-off.

US-H-1.0Pro: hip, in the flexion direction. Our guide to hip, knee and ankle exoskeletons compares the three.

#### 2. Peak torque

Torque is rotational force at the joint, measured in newton-metres (Nm). The peak figure is the most the motor delivers at any moment. Higher is not automatically better: beyond what the joint needs, extra torque adds motor weight and battery drain, and badly timed torque feels like a shove.

US-H-1.0Pro: 16 Nm peak at the hip. Our 16 Nm explainer covers what that feels like.

#### 3. Weight, and where it sits

Check whether the weight includes the battery, and where on the body it rests. Weight at the waist is carried by the pelvis and feels lighter than the same weight further down the leg, which has to be swung with every step.

US-H-1.0Pro: 2.4 kg total, worn at the waist, foldable. See is 2.4 kg heavy for an exoskeleton?

#### 4. Assistance time per charge

Battery figures are usually quoted in hours of assistance. That number is only meaningful with terrain attached: stairs and steep slopes draw much more than flat pavement. Look for whether the figure is "up to" and what kind of use it assumes.

US-H-1.0Pro: up to 4 hours of assistance.

#### 5. Charge time

Often overlooked, but it decides whether the device is ready again after lunch. A short charge time matters more than a slightly bigger battery if you use the device in two blocks each day.

US-H-1.0Pro: 2 hours to a full charge.


#### 6. Ingress protection (IP rating)

The IP code is a standard rating for protection against solids (first digit) and water (second digit). In a tropical climate it decides whether you can keep walking when the rain starts.

US-H-1.0Pro: IP54, meaning dust-protected and resistant to splashing water from any direction. It is not rated for immersion or pressure jets. Our IP54 guide reads the two digits in detail.

#### 7. Controls and modes

How do you start it, and do you have to change settings while walking? Some devices need an app; some need manual mode changes for stairs. Fewer decisions while walking usually means more consistent use, especially for older users.

US-H-1.0Pro: one button to start, no app needed to walk, terrain-adaptive mode switching, and posture detection that pauses assistance when you sit.

#### The line that is not a specification

Most spec sheets end with performance claims: percentages of load reduction, energy saving or range. For the US-H-1.0Pro, the manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step, up to 35% less energy on climbs, 30–50% less exertion on a daily commute and two to three times the walking range.

These are a different kind of number. A torque or weight figure describes the hardware. A performance percentage describes what happened to particular people, on particular terrain, under particular test conditions. They are useful for comparison only if you know how they were measured. Our guide to judging exoskeleton performance claims sets out the questions to ask.

#### What is often missing

- Price. For the US-H-1.0Pro in Singapore, pricing is quoted on request by the exclusive seller.
- Sizing range. Ask for waist and thigh ranges before booking.
- Classification. Whether the device is sold as a consumer product or registered as a medical device. The US-H-1.0Pro is a consumer mobility-assist device.


- Q: Which spec matters most for stairs?
  A: The joint assisted and how the torque is timed. Hip assistance targets the lift of the leg, which is where stairs cost the most. A high peak torque that arrives late does less than a modest one that arrives on time.
- Q: Should I compare battery life in hours or kilometres?
  A: Neither is reliable on its own. Ask what terrain the figure assumes. A stair-heavy day uses more energy than a flat one, whatever the unit.
- Q: Is a lighter exoskeleton always better?
  A: Not always. A lighter device may have less torque or less battery. Where the weight sits matters as much as the total.
- Q: Are the performance percentages measured specifications?
  A: No. They are manufacturer claims describing results under the maker's own test conditions. Treat them as "up to" figures, and test the device on your own route.

### Is 2.4 kg heavy for an exoskeleton? Where the weight sits

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-weight-explained/

Question: Is 2.4 kg heavy for a wearable exoskeleton?

Answer: Not for a powered device worn at the waist. 2.4 kg is a little more than a 2-litre bottle of water, and on the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro it rests on the pelvis rather than hanging from the shoulders or swinging at the ankle. Weight low on the leg costs much more energy to walk with than the same weight at the waist. The trade-off is that a lighter device usually means a smaller motor or battery, so total weight only makes sense next to torque and battery figures.

#### What 2.4 kg is, in everyday terms

2.4 kg is roughly a 2-litre bottle of water plus a mug, a medium bag of rice, or a laptop with its charger. Carried in your hand, you would notice it within a few minutes. Worn well, at the waist, most people stop noticing it once they are walking.

That difference between carrying and wearing is the whole story of exoskeleton weight.

#### Why where the weight sits matters more than how much

When you walk, your legs swing forward with every step. Anything attached low on the leg, such as a heavy shoe or an ankle weight, has to be accelerated and stopped with each stride. It is well established in walking research that added mass is more costly the further it sits from the body's centre, which is why runners care so much about shoe weight.

Weight at the waist, by contrast, moves with the body's centre of mass. It still has to be carried up stairs and slopes, but it does not have to be swung back and forth. That is why a hip-mounted device can weigh more than an ankle brace and still feel lighter in use.

- At the waist: carried by the pelvis, moves with the body, least costly.
- On the thigh: swung with each step, but close to the hip.
- At the knee or ankle: swung through the widest arc, most costly per gram.

The US-H-1.0Pro puts its motors and battery at the hip, with only short links along the thigh.

#### Weight against what it does

Total weight is meaningless on its own. An unpowered brace can be very light because it has no motor or battery. A powered device must carry both. So compare weight together with:

- Peak torque: 16 Nm for the US-H-1.0Pro.
- Assistance time: up to 4 hours per charge.
- Charge time: 2 hours.

A device that is half the weight but delivers far less assistance or runs out after an hour is not lighter in any way that matters. Our spec-sheet guide shows how these lines relate.


#### What happens to the weight when you are being assisted

While the device is working, it adds assistance at the hip as each leg lifts. The manufacturer claims up to 80% less lower-body load per step for this model. Treat that as a manufacturer claim; your own result depends on you, the terrain and the assistance level. Practically, on stairs and slopes most users feel the assistance far more than the weight.

#### And when the battery runs out

This is the honest test of any powered device. When the US-H-1.0Pro's battery runs out, it stops assisting but does not lock the legs. You keep walking normally, carrying 2.4 kg at your waist. That is noticeable on a long climb but not a hazard. Planning a charge around longer days avoids it; our battery guide covers how.

#### Weight for older users

For an older person, weight matters at two moments: putting the device on and carrying it when it is off. Worn at the waist and put on seated, 2.4 kg is manageable for most people after a fitting. Folded, it can sit on a shelf by the door or go in a tote bag. If lifting even that is difficult, a family member can help with putting it on. Our guide to putting it on seated explains the routine.

#### Weight for hikers and commuters

For a commuter, the question is whether it fits in a bag at the office: folded, it does. For a hiker, it is the trade between carrying 2.4 kg and having assistance on the climbs. Our trekking poles comparison looks at where those grams are earned back.

#### How to judge it yourself

Spec sheets cannot tell you how weight feels. At a fitting, walk the same short stretch twice: once with the device switched off, once switched on. The first tells you what the weight feels like; the second tells you whether the assistance outweighs it on your route.


- Q: Is the 2.4 kg including the battery?
  A: Yes. 2.4 kg is the total weight of the US-H-1.0Pro as worn.
- Q: Will the weight pull my trousers down or press on my back?
  A: The belt sits on the pelvis, not the waistband, and should be fitted snugly. If it slides or presses on the lower back, the fit needs adjusting; raise it with the team.
- Q: Is it heavy to carry when folded?
  A: It weighs the same 2.4 kg folded, about the same as a laptop with its charger, and fits in a daypack or tote bag.
- Q: Do lighter exoskeletons exist?
  A: Unpowered devices can be lighter because they have no motor or battery. Among powered devices, compare weight together with torque and battery figures rather than on its own.

### "Up to 80%": how to read exoskeleton performance claims

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/how-to-judge-exoskeleton-performance-claims/

Question: How should you read exoskeleton performance claims like "up to 80% less load"?

Answer: As the best result under the manufacturer's own test conditions, not as what you will personally get. "Up to" sets a ceiling, not an average. A useful claim tells you what was measured, how, on whom, on what terrain and against what comparison. For the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro, the 80% load reduction, 35% climbing energy saving, 30–50% commute exertion reduction and 2–3× range are manufacturer claims. The fairest test is your own route, walked with and without the device.

#### Why this guide exists on a seller's website

ExoStride's own pages quote performance figures. We think the people reading them deserve to know how to read them, including ours. Every brand in this category publishes percentages, and very few explain what is behind them. That leaves buyers, families and physiotherapists either believing everything or believing nothing. Neither is useful.

#### Two kinds of number

An exoskeleton spec sheet mixes two different kinds of figure:

- Specifications describe the hardware: 16 Nm peak torque, 2.4 kg, IP54, up to 4 hours of assistance, 2-hour charge. They can be checked on the device.
- Performance claims describe what happened to people using it: less load, less energy, more range. They depend on who was tested, where, how and against what.

The US-H-1.0Pro's performance figures are manufacturer claims: up to 80% less lower-body load per step, up to 35% less energy on climbs, 30–50% less exertion on a daily commute and two to three times the walking range. Every page on this site labels them that way.

#### What "up to" really means

"Up to 80%" means that 80% was the best result observed or achievable under the conditions used. It does not mean the average, and it does not mean the typical user. A range such as "30–50%" is more informative, because it admits variation, but it still depends on conditions.

When you see "up to", read it as: under the right conditions, it can be this much. Then ask what those conditions were.

#### Five questions to ask about any claim

- What was measured? Load on a joint, energy used, distance walked and perceived effort are all different things, measured in different ways.
- How was it measured? In a laboratory with instruments, outdoors with a wearable sensor, or by asking users how it felt?
- Who was tested? Young healthy adults, older adults, people in rehabilitation? How many?
- On what terrain? Flat treadmill, stairs, an incline, a real commute?
- Compared with what? Walking without the device, walking with it switched off, or walking with a different device?

A brand that can answer these is giving you something you can weigh. A brand that cannot is giving you an advertisement. Ask the ExoStride team the same questions; that is a fair request.


#### Lab results and real life

Laboratory measurements are controlled, which makes them good for comparison and poor at predicting daily life. Real routes include heat, crowds, carrying bags, stopping at traffic lights and walking more slowly than on a treadmill. That usually narrows the difference. On the other hand, real life also contains the steepest stairs and the longest walks, which is often where assistance matters most.

Our guide to how energy savings are measured explains the most common laboratory method in plain language.

#### Testimonials are not evidence, but your experience is

Individual stories can be honest and still unrepresentative. This site does not publish testimonials as proof. What you can trust is a careful comparison you make yourself:

- Pick one route you walk often.
- Walk it once without the device and once with it, on similar days.
- Record time, rest stops, stairs climbed and how tired you felt on a 0 to 10 scale.
- Repeat over a few weeks.

Our guide to tracking progress in the first month has a simple log for this.

#### Red flags in any exoskeleton marketing

- Medical-sounding promises from a product that is not registered as a medical device.
- Claims of curing, treating or reversing a condition.
- A single headline percentage with no mention of terrain or conditions.
- Before-and-after stories with no way of knowing what else changed.
- Pressure to buy without a trial on your own route.

#### How we label our own figures

On this site, every ExoStride performance figure is described as a manufacturer claim for the US-H-1.0Pro, and the footer of every page repeats that the figures vary with user, terrain and assistance level. Measured specifications, such as 16 Nm, 2.4 kg, IP54, up to 4 hours and 2 hours, are listed separately. If you ever find a figure on this site that is not labelled that way, tell us and we will fix it.


- Q: Are ExoStride's performance figures independently verified?
  A: They are manufacturer claims for the US-H-1.0Pro, and we label them that way. Ask the Singapore team what was measured and how; the honest test is a fitting on your own route.
- Q: What is the difference between less load and less energy?
  A: Load refers to the force the body's joints and muscles handle with each step. Energy refers to how much the body burns to walk, usually measured through breathing. They are related but measured differently, so the percentages are not interchangeable.
- Q: Why do different brands' percentages vary so much?
  A: Because they measure different things, on different people, on different terrain. Two percentages from different test conditions cannot be compared directly.
- Q: What is the most reliable way to judge an exoskeleton?
  A: Walk your own route with and without it, several times, and write down the results. That tells you more about your situation than any headline figure.

### How exoskeleton energy savings are measured: metabolic cost

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-metabolic-cost-explained/

Question: How do researchers measure whether an exoskeleton saves energy?

Answer: Usually by measuring breathing. The standard lab method, indirect calorimetry, uses a mask to record how much oxygen a person takes in and how much carbon dioxide they breathe out while walking at a steady pace. From that, the energy spent per minute is calculated and compared with and without the device. That number is the "metabolic cost". Results depend heavily on speed, slope, the person and how long they have practised with the device, which is why claims such as the US-H-1.0Pro's "up to 35% less energy on climbs" are manufacturer claims, not guarantees.

#### What "metabolic cost" means

Every step you take burns energy. Muscles convert fuel into movement, and that process uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. The total energy your body spends to walk a given distance or for a given time is called the metabolic cost of walking.

When an exoskeleton brand says its device reduces energy use, it is almost always talking about this number: how much less energy the body spends to do the same walk.

#### How it is measured in a lab

The most widely used method in research is indirect calorimetry. In plain terms:

- The person wears a mask connected to a gas analyser, often a portable unit carried on the back.
- They walk at a fixed speed, often on a treadmill, sometimes at a set incline.
- The analyser measures how much oxygen they breathe in and how much carbon dioxide they breathe out, breath by breath.
- After a few minutes the readings settle into a steady state. Those minutes are used for the calculation.
- The same walk is repeated with and without the device, and the energy per minute is compared.

Researchers usually subtract the energy spent standing still, so the result reflects the cost of walking itself. The percentage difference between the two conditions is the headline "energy saving".

#### Why results vary so much

Metabolic cost is sensitive. Small changes in conditions move the result:

- Speed: walking faster changes the cost and the share an exoskeleton can save.
- Slope and stairs: climbing costs far more than walking on the flat, so there is more to save. This is why claims for climbs are often higher than for level ground.
- The person: fitness, body size and how they walk all change the baseline.
- Practice: people often need time to adapt to assistance. Results on the first day can differ from results after several sessions.
- Comparison: compared with walking without the device, or with the device worn but switched off? The second comparison includes the cost of carrying it.

Two studies with different conditions can produce very different percentages for similar devices. That is not necessarily anyone being dishonest; it is the nature of the measurement.


#### Reading the ExoStride figure

For the US-H-1.0Pro, the manufacturer claims up to 35% less energy on steep, sustained climbs, along with up to 80% less lower-body load per step, 30–50% less exertion on a daily commute and two to three times the walking range. These are manufacturer claims for this model. "Up to" means the figure is a ceiling under favourable conditions, not what every user will measure.

The questions worth asking about it, or any other brand's figure, are the ones in our guide to judging exoskeleton performance claims: what was measured, how, on whom, on what terrain and against what comparison.

#### Effort is not the same as energy

Lab energy and how hard a walk feels are related but not identical. People often report a bigger difference in perceived effort than the gas analyser shows, or the other way round. For most buyers, how tiring the walk feels is the more useful measure anyway, and it is easy to record yourself on a 0 to 10 scale.

#### Measuring it yourself, roughly

You cannot run indirect calorimetry at home, but you can make a fair, rough comparison on a climb:

- Choose a steady climb you know, such as a long staircase or a hill path.
- Walk it at the same pace twice on similar days: once without assistance, once with.
- Note your heart rate at the top if you have a watch, your time, and your effort score.
- Rest fully between attempts, or do them on separate days.

Heart rate is a rough proxy for effort and is affected by heat, sleep and caffeine, so look for consistent differences over several attempts. Our Bukit Timah Hill comparison walks through a structured version.

#### Why timing matters to energy

An exoskeleton only saves energy if it helps at the right moment. Assistance that arrives late can make walking harder. That is why control matters as much as torque; our 16 Nm explainer covers it.


- Q: Is metabolic cost the same as calories burned?
  A: They are closely related. Metabolic cost is the energy the body spends, which can be expressed in calories. Lab studies usually report it in watts or per kilogram of body weight.
- Q: Why are energy savings higher on climbs?
  A: Climbing costs much more energy than walking on the flat, and much of that cost comes from lifting the leg and body. There is more effort to remove, so the percentage that assistance can save is often larger.
- Q: Can I measure it with a smartwatch?
  A: Not precisely. A watch estimates energy from heart rate and movement. It is useful for rough comparisons on the same route, but it is not a lab measurement.
- Q: Does the 35% figure apply to walking on flat ground?
  A: No. The manufacturer's 35% claim refers to steep, sustained climbs. On flat ground, the commute figure of 30–50% less exertion is the relevant manufacturer claim.

### Powered vs passive exoskeletons: what is the difference?

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/powered-vs-passive-exoskeleton/

Question: What is the difference between a powered and a passive exoskeleton?

Answer: A passive exoskeleton has no motor. It uses springs, elastic bands or counterweights to store energy in one part of a movement and give it back in another, so it can only return energy you put in. A powered exoskeleton has motors, sensors and a battery, so it can add energy at a chosen moment. For walking up stairs and slopes, where the body has to lift itself, adding energy at the right moment is the key difference. Passive devices are simpler, lighter and need no charging.

#### Two families of exoskeleton

The word exoskeleton covers a wide range of devices, from spring-loaded vests used in factories to motorised suits used in research. For anyone choosing one for walking, the first split to understand is between passive and powered.

#### How a passive exoskeleton works

A passive, or unpowered, exoskeleton has no motor and no battery. It works with mechanical elements:

- Springs that compress or stretch in one phase of a movement and release in another.
- Elastic bands that resist one direction and assist the return.
- Clutches or locks that hold a position, such as a supported crouch.

The key physical point is that a passive device cannot add energy overall. It can only store energy you put in and return it at another moment, or redirect load to a different part of the body. In industrial settings that is very useful: a passive shoulder exoskeleton can transfer the weight of raised arms to the hips for hours of overhead work.

#### How a powered exoskeleton works

A powered, or active, exoskeleton adds three things:

- Motors (actuators) at one or more joints that can add torque.
- Sensors that read movement, such as joint angle and the timing of each step.
- A controller and battery that decide when and how much torque to deliver.

Because it has a power source, a powered device can put energy into a movement at the moment it is needed. The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a powered hip exoskeleton: it reads your gait and adds up to 16 Nm of torque at the hip as each leg lifts (spec-sheet figure), and changes its assistance automatically between level ground, stairs and slopes. Our guide to how exoskeletons sense gait explains the sensing side.


#### Why the difference matters for walking

On flat ground, walking is already quite efficient, and much of each step recovers energy naturally. Climbing is different. Going up stairs or a slope, the body has to raise its own weight, and that energy has to come from somewhere. A passive device can help redistribute effort, but it cannot supply the extra energy that lifting requires. A powered device can.

That is why stairs, overhead bridges and hill paths are where powered hip assistance is most noticeable. For the US-H-1.0Pro, the manufacturer claims up to 35% less energy on climbs and up to 80% less lower-body load per step; those are manufacturer claims, and results vary with the person and terrain.

#### Side by side

- Energy: passive stores and returns; powered can add.
- Timing: passive responds to your movement mechanically; powered decides when to assist based on sensors.
- Adaptation: passive behaves the same everywhere; powered can change its profile for stairs and slopes.
- Weight: passive is usually lighter; powered carries motors and a battery (2.4 kg in total for the US-H-1.0Pro).
- Charging: passive needs none; powered needs charging (2 hours to full for the US-H-1.0Pro).
- Failure mode: passive keeps working; a powered device stops assisting when the battery is flat. The US-H-1.0Pro does not lock the legs when that happens.
- Water: both can be affected; check the IP rating on powered devices. The US-H-1.0Pro is IP54.

#### Which suits you

A passive device can make sense for repetitive, predictable work tasks, or where charging is impractical. For walking in daily life, especially with stairs and slopes, a powered device that adds energy at the right moment is usually the more useful category. Whichever you consider, compare the joint assisted, weight, battery and controls; our spec-sheet guide walks through each line. The joint matters too: see our comparison of hip, knee and ankle exoskeletons.

#### A note on names

Brands use many terms: active, robotic, motorised, wearable robot, smart exoskeleton. In practice, if a device has a battery and a motor, it is powered. If it has neither, it is passive. Some hybrid designs use small motors only to adjust a spring or lock; ask what the motor actually does.


- Q: Can a passive exoskeleton help me climb stairs?
  A: It can redistribute some effort, but it cannot add the energy needed to lift your body. Powered devices are designed to add assistance at that moment.
- Q: Are powered exoskeletons safe if the battery dies?
  A: That depends on the device. The US-H-1.0Pro stops assisting but does not lock your legs, so you keep walking normally, carrying 2.4 kg.
- Q: Is a powered exoskeleton a robot?
  A: In a loose sense, yes: it senses, decides and acts. In practice it is a wearable assist device that responds to your own movement rather than moving you on its own.
- Q: Do passive exoskeletons need fitting?
  A: Yes. Any exoskeleton needs to fit well to transfer force comfortably. Powered devices also need their assistance level set, which is part of a fitting.

### Hip, knee or ankle exoskeleton: which joint should be assisted?

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/hip-vs-knee-vs-ankle-exoskeleton/

Question: Is a hip, knee or ankle exoskeleton best for walking?

Answer: It depends on what makes walking hard. Hip devices help lift the leg forward, which is where stairs, slopes and long walks cost the most effort, and they keep the weight high on the body. Knee devices are usually about support and extension, for example rising from a chair or controlling a bent knee. Ankle devices assist push-off at the end of each step. For stamina on stairs and longer routes, hip assistance is often the most efficient choice; for knee instability or foot drop, a clinician may point elsewhere.

#### Each joint does a different job in a step

Walking looks simple, but each joint has its own role in every stride:

- The ankle pushes off at the end of the step, propelling the body forward.
- The knee bends to swing the leg through, then straightens and absorbs the shock as the foot lands.
- The hip swings the whole leg forward and, on stairs or slopes, lifts it up against gravity.

An exoskeleton that assists one joint changes one part of this sequence. Choosing a device is mostly about matching that part to the problem.

#### Hip exoskeletons

A hip exoskeleton sits at the waist with links down the thigh and assists the movement of the thigh, usually as the leg swings forward and lifts (flexion), and sometimes as it pushes back (extension).

- Strongest case: stairs, slopes, overhead bridges and long walks, where lifting the leg is what tires you.
- Weight: carried at the pelvis, close to the body's centre, which makes it less costly to walk with.
- Knee: left free, so its natural shock absorption is untouched.
- Limits: it does not support a knee that gives way or an ankle that drops.

The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a hip device. It adds up to 16 Nm in the flexion direction (spec-sheet figure), reads the gait continuously and switches profile automatically between level ground, stairs and steep terrain. Our 16 Nm explainer covers why the hip gives the most assistance per gram.

#### Knee exoskeletons and braces

Powered knee devices assist extension, for instance when standing up or climbing a step, or help control the knee as it bends. Unpowered knee braces mostly provide support and stability.

- Strongest case: knee weakness, a knee that buckles, or rising from a chair.
- Weight: sits mid-leg and is swung with every step, so each gram costs more.
- Limits: it does less for the effort of lifting the whole leg.

If the knee itself is the problem, a doctor or physiotherapist should guide the choice. Our knee brace and hip assist comparison for hiking covers the outdoor version of this question.


#### Ankle exoskeletons

Ankle devices assist push-off, or in some designs lift the toes during swing. They have been widely studied in research labs because the ankle produces a lot of the power in each step.

- Strongest case: weak push-off, or toes catching the ground.
- Weight: right at the end of the leg, the most costly place to carry mass.
- Limits: footwear and fit become critical; they can be harder to put on.

Foot drop and similar problems are clinical issues; a physiotherapist or orthotist is the right person to advise.

#### Matching the joint to the problem

- "Stairs and slopes wear me out." Hip.
- "I can walk, but not as far as I used to." Hip, often.
- "My knee gives way or hurts." See a doctor; knee support may be relevant.
- "My toes catch, or my foot slaps down." See a physiotherapist; ankle support may be relevant.
- "I lose my balance." None of these is a balance aid; a stick or frame and balance training come first.

#### What about multi-joint exoskeletons?

Full-leg exoskeletons that assist the hip, knee and ankle together exist, mostly for clinical rehabilitation of people who cannot walk unaided. They are heavier and more complex and are usually used under supervision. For everyday walking by people who can already walk, a single-joint device is lighter and simpler.

#### Weight follows the joint

The further from the hip a device sits, the more each gram costs to walk with, because it must be swung with every step. Our guide to exoskeleton weight explains why a hip device can weigh more and still feel lighter. Whether the device is powered or passive matters too; see powered vs passive exoskeletons.


- Q: Will a hip exoskeleton help my knee pain?
  A: It is not designed to treat knee pain. It reduces the effort of lifting the leg, which some people find makes walking easier overall, but if your knee hurts, see a doctor or physiotherapist about the cause first.
- Q: Why do many walking exoskeletons assist the hip?
  A: On stairs and slopes, the hip does much of the expensive work of lifting the leg, and hardware at the waist is cheaper to carry than hardware lower down the leg.
- Q: Can I wear a knee brace with a hip exoskeleton?
  A: Often, yes, as long as the brace does not interfere with the thigh links. Bring it to the fitting and ask your physiotherapist whether you still need it.
- Q: Which type is best for older adults?
  A: For older adults whose main problem is stamina on stairs and longer routes, hip assistance is a common fit. If balance or a specific joint problem is the issue, a clinician should guide the choice.

### How does an exoskeleton know when to help? Gait sensing explained

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/how-exoskeletons-sense-gait/

Question: How does a powered exoskeleton know when to help you?

Answer: By reading your movement continuously. Sensors track how your thighs are moving and where you are in each step; a controller recognises the pattern of walking, climbing or sitting and releases torque at the moment the hip starts to lift. The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro does this automatically: it reads the gait, delivers assistance inside the flexion window, switches profile between level ground, stairs and steep terrain, and pauses when you sit. There is nothing to adjust while walking.

#### The problem every powered exoskeleton has to solve

A motor at the hip can push the thigh forward. The hard part is knowing when. Push a fraction too early or too late and the assistance fights your stride instead of helping it. Push the same way on a staircase as on a flat pavement and it feels wrong on one or the other. Push while you are sitting down and it is a nuisance.

So the real intelligence of a powered exoskeleton is not in its motor. It is in how it reads your walking.

#### What the sensors measure

Wearable exoskeletons commonly use some combination of:

- Joint angle sensors, which measure how far the thigh has swung relative to the pelvis.
- Inertial measurement units (IMUs), small chips like those in a phone that measure acceleration and rotation.
- Motor feedback, which tells the controller how the joint is moving and how much force is being applied.

Together these give a picture, many times a second, of where each leg is in the walking cycle. Exact sensor designs differ between manufacturers and are not usually published in detail.

#### From readings to a decision

The controller turns those readings into decisions:

- Phase: where am I in the step? The moment that matters most for hip assistance is when the leg begins to swing forward and lift, the flexion window.
- Activity: am I walking on the flat, climbing stairs, going up a slope, going down, standing still or sitting?
- Amount: how much assistance does this activity call for, within the level set at the fitting?

For the US-H-1.0Pro, the published behaviour is that it reads gait continuously, releases torque inside the flexion window, switches assistance profile between level ground, stairs and steep terrain on its own, and uses posture detection to pause when you sit. Peak torque is 16 Nm on the spec sheet.


#### Why timing beats strength

A useful way to picture it: a friend gives your thigh a well-timed nudge forward and up each time you start to step. A gentle nudge at the right moment helps. A strong shove at the wrong moment throws you off. This is why a high peak torque on a spec sheet means little without good timing, and why people sometimes switch off devices that feel pushy. Our 16 Nm explainer goes into the numbers.

#### What changes on stairs, slopes and descents

- Level ground: assistance is light. Many users describe it as walking on ground that slopes slightly downhill.
- Stairs and climbs: each step requires lifting the leg higher against gravity, so assistance ramps up. This is where the manufacturer's claim of up to 35% less energy on climbs applies; it is a manufacturer claim and results vary.
- Descent: going down is a control problem, not a power problem. The US-H-1.0Pro reduces assistance so it never pushes you forward, and the handrail remains your main aid.

#### Sitting, standing and stopping

Posture detection pauses assistance when you sit and resumes when you stand. That makes a bench at the bus stop or a seat on the train uneventful. Our guide to sitting on the MRT or bus with an exoskeleton covers the practical side.

#### Why there is no app needed to walk

If a device needs you to choose a mode before a staircase, you have to think about the device instead of the stairs. Automatic switching removes that step. The US-H-1.0Pro starts with one button, and the optional app is used only for settings. That design matters most for older users and for anyone who simply wants to walk.

#### What it cannot sense

- It does not sense balance problems or catch a fall.
- It does not know your destination or how tired you are.
- It does not detect a slippery surface; grip is down to your shoes and the handrail.

#### Powered versus passive

This kind of sensing is what separates powered devices from passive spring-based ones, which respond mechanically and cannot change behaviour between terrain types. See powered vs passive exoskeletons.


- Q: How long does it take to adapt to my walking?
  A: The device reads your gait from the first steps. Most people take a few walks to get used to the feel; the fitting sets an assistance level that suits you to start with.
- Q: What if I walk unevenly or slowly?
  A: Gait sensing works on your own pattern rather than an ideal one. If the assistance feels mistimed, tell the fitting team; the assistance level can be adjusted.
- Q: Does it know when I am going downstairs?
  A: It reduces assistance on descent so it never pushes you forward. Always use the handrail on stairs.
- Q: Can I turn the automatic switching off?
  A: The device is designed so that walking needs no settings. Ask the team about what can be adjusted in the optional app.

### Medical vs consumer exoskeleton: what the label means in Singapore

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/medical-vs-consumer-exoskeleton-singapore/

Question: Is a powered exoskeleton a medical device in Singapore?

Answer: It depends on how it is made and what it is sold to do. Devices intended to diagnose, treat or rehabilitate a medical condition are regulated as medical devices, which in Singapore falls under the Health Sciences Authority (HSA). Consumer mobility-assist devices are sold to make walking easier, without medical claims. The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is a consumer mobility-assist device: no prescription is needed, and it does not diagnose or treat any condition. That is also why it should be used alongside, not instead of, medical care.

#### Why the label matters

Two exoskeletons can look similar and be sold under completely different rules. One is a medical device, with a stated medical purpose and the regulatory process that comes with it. The other is a consumer product, sold to make an everyday activity easier. The difference affects what the seller can claim, who can buy it, how it is used and what you should expect from it.

#### What makes something a medical device

In general terms, a product is a medical device when its manufacturer intends it to be used for a medical purpose, such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring, treating or alleviating a disease or injury, or compensating for or rehabilitating an injury or disability. The intended purpose, as described by the manufacturer, is central.

Exoskeletons sold for clinical gait rehabilitation, often used in hospitals under the supervision of therapists, typically fall into this group.

#### Who regulates medical devices in Singapore

In Singapore, medical devices are regulated by the Health Sciences Authority (HSA). Medical devices generally need to be registered before they can be supplied, with requirements that depend on the device's risk class. If a seller describes an exoskeleton as a medical device, it is reasonable to ask about its registration status.

This guide is a plain-language overview, not legal advice. HSA's own website is the authoritative source on the current rules.

#### What a consumer mobility-assist device is

A consumer device is sold for general use, without a medical purpose. In the case of a powered hip exoskeleton, that means making walking, stairs and longer routes less tiring for people who can already walk.

The ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro is sold in Singapore as a consumer mobility-assist device. Practically, that means:

- No prescription is needed to buy or use it.
- It is used at home, on the commute and outdoors, without clinical supervision.
- It does not diagnose, treat or cure any condition, and we do not claim that it does.
- Its performance figures (up to 80% less lower-body load per step, up to 35% less energy on climbs, 30–50% less commute exertion, 2–3× range) are manufacturer claims, not clinical outcomes.


#### What the consumer label does not mean

It does not mean the device is a toy, or that safety does not matter. It does mean that judgements about your health remain with your doctor and physiotherapist. If you are recovering from surgery, injury or illness, or if a doctor has advised caution about exercise, ask them before using any walking assist device. Our guide to who a hip exoskeleton is not for lists the common situations.

#### How to read medical-sounding marketing

Across the industry, consumer products sometimes borrow clinical language. Watch for:

- Words such as treats, cures, heals, reverses or prevents attached to a condition.
- Claims of being "clinically proven" without saying what was tested, on whom and where it was published.
- Before-and-after stories presented as evidence.

A consumer device should talk about what it helps you do, not what it does to a disease. Our guide to judging performance claims has more questions to ask.

#### Using a consumer device alongside therapy

Many people use a consumer exoskeleton in daily life while continuing physiotherapy. That can work well when the physiotherapist knows about it and helps set goals. Our guide for physiotherapists explains what the device does in clinical terms, so the conversation is easier.

#### Funding and insurance

Because classification affects how a product is treated by funding schemes and insurers, do not assume that a consumer device is covered by any medical subsidy or policy. Check directly with the scheme or insurer before buying.

#### Questions to ask any seller about classification

- Is this device sold as a medical device or as a consumer product?
- If it is a medical device, is it registered with HSA, and for what intended purpose?
- If it is a consumer product, does the seller make any medical claims about it?
- Does the device need a prescription or clinical supervision to use?

Clear answers to these four questions tell you how to read everything else on the box.


- Q: Do I need a doctor's prescription to buy ExoStride?
  A: No. It is a consumer mobility-assist device. If you have a health condition, recent surgery or injury, talk to your doctor or physiotherapist before using it.
- Q: Can a physiotherapist recommend a consumer device?
  A: Yes. Physiotherapists often advise on consumer equipment. The decision about whether it suits your recovery is theirs and yours together.
- Q: Is a medical exoskeleton better than a consumer one?
  A: Not necessarily; they are designed for different jobs. Clinical exoskeletons are often used to help people who cannot walk unaided, under supervision. A consumer hip device is designed for people who can walk but find it tiring.
- Q: Will my insurance or a subsidy cover it?
  A: Do not assume so. Coverage depends on the scheme or policy and on how a product is classified. Check with them directly before buying.

### How a hip exoskeleton should fit: sizing, straps and pressure points

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-fit-and-sizing/

Question: How should a hip exoskeleton fit?

Answer: Snug, low and aligned. The belt should sit low on the pelvis, not on the soft waist or the ribs, firm enough not to slide but loose enough to breathe and sit comfortably. The device's hip joints should line up with your own hip joints at the side. Thigh straps should hold the links against the outside of each thigh with room for two fingers underneath. A good fit is what turns torque into useful assistance; a poor fit wastes it and causes rubbing.

#### Why fit decides how well it works

A powered hip exoskeleton passes force from its motors to your legs through two contact points: the belt at the pelvis and the straps at the thighs. If those contact points move, slip or press in the wrong place, some of the assistance is lost as the device shifts instead of your leg moving. It can also feel as though the timing is off, when the real problem is fit.

That is why the Singapore team does a guided fitting before first use, and why it is worth knowing what a good fit looks like.

#### The belt: low and firm

- Position: on the bony part of the pelvis, around the top of the hips. Not on the soft waist, and nowhere near the ribs.
- Tightness: firm enough that it does not slide up when you walk or climb stairs, but you can breathe deeply and sit comfortably.
- Clothing: over a single layer is best. Thick waistbands, belts with large buckles and bulky pockets under the belt create pressure points.

If the belt rides up as you walk, it is usually too loose or sitting too high to begin with.

#### The hip joints: aligned with yours

The device has a joint at each side of the hip. For the assistance to feel natural, those joints should sit level with your own hip joints, roughly at the side of the hip where the thigh bone meets the pelvis. If they sit too high or too low, the thigh link moves in a slightly different arc from your thigh, which can rub and make the push feel awkward.

#### The thigh straps: secure, not tight

- Position: on the outside of the thigh, above the knee, with the link lying flat along the leg.
- Tightness: two fingers should slide underneath. Too tight restricts circulation and leaves marks; too loose lets the link rotate.
- Check: when you walk, the link should stay on the outside of the thigh rather than drifting to the front.


#### What a good fit feels like

- After a few minutes of walking, you stop noticing the belt.
- On stairs, the assistance feels like a nudge at the thigh rather than a tug at the waist.
- Sitting down is comfortable without loosening anything.
- After taking it off, any marks fade within a few minutes.

Our 16 Nm explainer describes what well-timed assistance should feel like once the fit is right.

#### Signs the fit needs adjusting

- Red marks or sore spots that last more than twenty minutes after taking it off.
- The belt sliding up, or pressing into the lower back.
- Thigh links rotating to the front or back of the leg.
- Rubbing at the side of the hip.
- Assistance that feels like a shove or a tug rather than a nudge.

Do not put up with any of these. Contact the team; most are fixed by small adjustments.

#### Sizing before you book

Fit depends on waist, hip and thigh measurements and on the configuration supplied in Singapore. Before booking a fitting, it helps to have a rough idea of your measurements and to ask the team whether they fall in the device's range. The fitting confirms it.

#### Fit for older users and limited mobility

For older users, the priority is a fit that can be repeated every day without help. The team can set strap lengths so that daily use is mostly fastening rather than adjusting. Our step-by-step guide to putting it on seated is built around this.

#### Fit and weight

A good fit also changes how heavy the device feels. 2.4 kg resting firmly on the pelvis feels very different from 2.4 kg sliding around. Our guide to exoskeleton weight covers where weight should sit.

#### Sharing a device

The belt and thigh links adjust, so two people can physically share a unit. In practice, sizing has to be readjusted with each swap, which adds friction. If two people in a household would use it daily, raise it at the fitting.


- Q: What should I wear to the fitting?
  A: What you will usually wear when using it: for example, trousers or shorts and a light top, with the shoes you walk in. Avoid a thick belt or bulky pockets at the waist.
- Q: Can I wear it over a dress or sarong?
  A: Possibly; loose fabric can bunch under the straps. Try it at the fitting with your usual clothing.
- Q: Will it fit if I lose or gain weight?
  A: The belt and straps adjust within a range. Significant changes in body size may need a refit; contact the team.
- Q: Can I adjust the fit myself later?
  A: Yes, the straps are adjustable. If the fit keeps changing or something rubs, ask the team rather than over-tightening.

### Before you buy an exoskeleton: 12 questions to ask the seller

URL: https://exostride.sg/guides/exoskeleton-buying-checklist-questions/

Question: What should you ask before buying a powered exoskeleton?

A good seller answers plainly and puts it in writing. For the ExoStride US-H-1.0Pro in Singapore, the exclusive seller is HT Science & Development Pte. Ltd.

#### Why a checklist helps

Powered exoskeletons are a new category for most buyers. There is no familiar reference point, as there is for a phone or a washing machine, and the person buying is often an adult child buying for a parent. A short list of questions keeps the conversation focused on what matters and makes it easy to compare answers.

- 11. Who services it in Singapore, and what does the warranty cover? Ask for warranty length, what is excluded, how repairs are handled and how long they take, and whether a replacement is available meanwhile. Get it in writing.

#### What good answers sound like

Good answers are specific, admit limits and come with paperwork. "It depends" is fine if it is followed by what it depends on. Be cautious of answers that promise medical results, avoid the trial question or push for a decision on the day.

Bring your parent into the conversation, not just the decision. Our caregiver's guide covers how to raise the idea and what to check at the fitting.

Write the answers down as you go, ideally on the same sheet as this list, and ask the seller to confirm the important ones by message or email. If you are comparing two devices, use the same twelve questions for both, in the same order. Differences that look small in a showroom, such as a charge time, a sizing range or a return period, often decide how well a device fits daily life. And if you are buying on behalf of someone else, read the answers back to them before deciding; they are the one who will wear it.
